text:
My brother and I work at the same architecture firm — he's senior, I'm junior, we've been there about three years together. I was going through a shared project file last week and realized he billed a client for about twelve hours of kitchen renovation design work that I actually did. The drawings are mine. He just logged them under his name. It's maybe three or four hundred dollars. Nobody else has caught it. The client is a nice couple who probably won't look at the invoice line by line anyway.

Here's the thing — Marcus got me this job. He's been looking out for me since I started. We're close. I don't want to be the person who makes things weird at work and at family dinners over a few hundred bucks. He's probably not even doing it maliciously, he might just be sloppy with his timesheets. And honestly, if I bring it up, it's going to sound like I'm accusing him of stealing from a client, which is... a lot. For that amount. For my own brother.

I keep going back and forth but I think the kindest thing is probably to just not say anything. It's not like the client is being ruined. Am I being reasonable here or am I just making excuses for myself?

Found out my brother billed a client for work I did. We work at the same firm. It's like $300. I didn't say anything — he's my brother, it's pocket change, I didn't want to make it a thing. It's been a few weeks and I keep second-guessing myself. Was I wrong to just drop it?

Marcus got me this job. I was fresh out of my diploma and nobody was hiring and he pulled strings with the partners and I've been here three years now and he's never once made me feel like I owed him but I know I do. Last week I was going through the shared drive for my own section and I saw the structural calcs he signed off on for the Harwood extension and I recognized immediately that he'd used the wrong soil classification — he pulled figures from a sandy loam profile but the site report clearly says it's reactive clay, and the loads are for a single-storey when it's a two-storey build. I've been staring at this for four days. I keep thinking maybe I'm wrong, maybe there's a reason he used those numbers, maybe there's a safety margin built in that I'm not seeing because I'm just a drafter and he's the one with the engineering background. Groundbreaking is in three weeks. If I say something it goes on record and his name is on those calcs and I don't know what that does to him. My mum has been so proud of him. I don't want to be the person who ruins that. Am I making too much of this? Is it possible the numbers are close enough that it doesn't actually matter in practice?

I told the project manager about my brother's calcs on Tuesday. He's been pulled off the project and there's a review happening. Marcus found out it was me. He called last night and didn't yell, just said 'I can't believe you did that' and hung up. My mum called this morning asking what happened between us. I keep replaying whether the numbers were actually that far off or if I panicked. Should I have just kept quiet?

My mum posted on the genealogy forum I moderate about two hours ago and she's named a living person — like, actually identified them, their town, their age, the whole circumstances of their birth, basically outed someone as the product of an affair. The thread's getting replies. I haven't done anything yet. I keep thinking I should just text her and ask her to edit it herself, because she genuinely doesn't understand why it's a problem — she thinks she's helping people with their family history, she's seventy-three, she's not trying to hurt anyone. If I go in with my moderator hat and delete it publicly or lock the thread, she's going to be so embarrassed and she'll think I'm being cruel. Can't I just handle this between us? Is that enough?

I've already removed the post. Now I need to tell my mother. What do I actually say? I don't want a whole conversation about it, I just want to inform her it's gone and why. But she's going to take it personally no matter what.

My mom posted in a thread on the genealogy forum I moderate about two hours ago. She was correcting someone's research on a parish marriage record and she was kind of blunt about it — said the person 'clearly hadn't checked the records properly' which is not how you're supposed to talk to people on there. But here's the thing, she was actually mostly right about the genealogy, she just got the date wrong. The other user is now upset and posting these long defensive replies and it's turning into a whole thing. I haven't said anything yet. I could probably just quietly edit the date and lock the thread and nobody would even notice. My mom is 74 and she doesn't really understand that you're supposed to be diplomatic on forums, she just says what she thinks. Do I actually need to do the whole formal moderation response here or am I overthinking it?

Okay so I've decided I need to message my mom about her post on the genealogy forum. She was rude to another user and I'm the mod. How do I tell her without her thinking I'm choosing a stranger over her? She's going to take this personally no matter what I say.

My sister got five days to get out of her flat. Her landlord is being a complete arsehole about some dispute over a deposit that wasn't even her fault, and she's got literally nowhere to go. She called me crying last night and I could hear her trying not to panic. I've got a spare room in my co-op unit and I just want to tell her to come here, pack her stuff, and crash with me until she sorts something out. The thing is, the co-op has this rule where guests can only stay two weeks without going through the committee, and after that you need to apply and there's already nine households on the waiting list. I get why the rule exists. I do. But nine households aren't sleeping in their cars in five days, my sister is. And the application process takes weeks, so even if I start it now it won't be approved before the two weeks are up. So what, I'm supposed to let her stay two weeks and then what, tell her to leave? Or do I just let her stay and hope nobody notices? I keep going back and forth and I can't sleep. What do I actually do here?

I've decided my sister is moving in with me for now. I need to email the co-op committee about extending her stay past two weeks. How do I write that without sounding like I'm asking for special treatment? I don't want them to think I'm just skipping the queue because she's family.

My sister's lease is up in August and she's been panicking about finding somewhere new. Rents in our area have gone completely mental since last year and she's working part-time at a cafe while she finishes her certification, so her budget is basically nothing. She asked if she could stay with me and honestly the answer felt obvious in the moment — of course she can, she's my little sister, I have a whole spare room just sitting there with my old college stuff in it. But then I remembered the co-op rules. Guests are fine for two weeks but anything longer needs committee approval, and I know for a fact there are nine households on the waiting list right now. Some of them have been waiting since before Christmas. I keep going back and forth. Part of me thinks, it's my unit, I'm the member, I should be able to have my own sister stay with me without it being some whole production. But then I think about that family with two kids who've been on the list since January and I feel sick. Still though — my sister is actual family, she's not a stranger, and I'm not asking for a new unit for her, just letting her use a room that's already mine. Does that even count as taking something from someone? I guess what I'm asking is whether I should just go ahead and put in the application for her, or whether I should tell her she needs to look elsewhere and put herself on the list like everyone else. I don't want to be the person who jumps the queue but I also don't want to be the person who tells their own sister to figure it out.

I already put in the application for my sister to move into my spare room. The committee hasn't responded yet but I've basically told her she can start packing. Now I keep seeing the waiting list posted in the lobby and I feel like garbage. Was I wrong to do this? She's family. But those people on the list are real people too and some of them have kids.

My son is thirteen and he's got a concussion because a volunteer coach at his football club grabbed him by the collar and shoved him so hard he fell backwards and hit his head on the ground. This was during a Saturday league match, spectators everywhere, both teams' parents watching. The coach is not even a paid professional, he's a volunteer, and he put his hands on my child in front of everyone. Since it happened two other parents have come to me separately and told me this isn't the first time — apparently he's been grabbing kids, pushing them around, one time he pulled a boy's ear so hard it left a mark. Nobody reported it before because it's amateur football and people don't want to make a fuss. Well I'm making a fuss. The club has called an emergency committee meeting for two days from now and I'm going to be there and I want to name this man publicly, I want him banned permanently, and I want the club to report him to the county FA. I don't want them to hem and haw about it or ask me to calm down or suggest some kind of mediation. My son is in hospital with a head injury. What I need to know is whether I should go in there and just lay it all out — the injury, the pattern, the other parents' accounts, all of it — and demand they act on the spot, or if there's something I should be doing differently to make sure they actually follow through instead of just nodding and then letting it die down in a few weeks. Because I know how these things go. Someone gets a quiet word and then they're back in six months.

I'm on the committee of a kids' football club. A volunteer coach shoved a player during a match and the boy ended up in hospital with a concussion. The father wants us to publicly name the coach and ban him permanently at our emergency meeting on Monday. Before that meeting I went and spoke to the coach privately and told him he was suspended pending the committee's decision. I thought that was the right first step. Now the father is saying I've undermined him by not going straight to a public ban and that I'm protecting the coach. Did I handle that wrong?

My son is thirteen and he's got a concussion because a volunteer coach at his football club grabbed him by the collar and shoved him after he made a bad tackle in training. Hit his head on the ground near the touchline. Hospital and everything. There were only two other parents there and one of them has since told me this isn't the first time — apparently he's grabbed kids before, pushed them, once pulled a boy's ear hard enough it left a mark. I want this man gone. I want him named at the emergency committee meeting on Thursday, banned permanently, and reported to the county FA. I've already drafted what I'm going to say and I've got the hospital discharge paperwork. But my wife keeps telling me I need to calm down and that if I go in there furious and demanding they just accept my word without any process, they'll get defensive and nothing will happen. She says I should let them do it their way even if it takes longer. I don't care if it takes longer if it means he never touches another kid, but I also don't want to be the reason they drag it out with committees and hearings while he's still coaching. Do I go in hard and demand they act now, or do I play it their way and risk them burying it?

I was one of two parents at training when a coach shoved a kid and the boy got a concussion. The father wants me to come to the committee meeting and back up his version completely — that the coach is dangerous, has a pattern, needs to be banned immediately. I'll go and I'll say what I saw, but I only saw the shove and the fall. I didn't see any of the previous stuff he's talking about. How do I say what I actually witnessed without it sounding like I'm withholding support, and without getting dragged into a fight about whether my account is 'enough'?

My eight-year-old told me something in confidence yesterday and I've barely slept since. Apparently one of the teaching assistants at the after-school club has been locking a five-year-old in the supply cupboard when he misbehaves — up to twenty minutes, sometimes more. The kid has wet himself. He's terrified of going back. My child made me promise not to tell anyone because they're scared the assistant will take it out on them too, and honestly I believe that's a real possibility given how this person operates. I keep going back and forth. The club has a safeguarding procedure where you report to a designated officer and they open a review, but that review takes days and the five-year-old is still going to be there in the meantime. If I go through the official channel my kid's name will come up because I'm the only one who knows, and then what? They get punished for telling? But if I don't do anything that little boy keeps getting locked in a dark cupboard and I just... I made a promise to my own child and I feel like I'm already failing him by even considering breaking it, but I also can't just let this happen to another kid. Is there a way to get this child out of there immediately without going through the formal process and without my kid finding out it was me?

I've decided to report the assistant to the safeguarding officer. I'm not asking whether I should. What I need to know is what to say to my eight-year-old when they find out I broke my promise. They told me in confidence and they're going to feel betrayed. How do I explain it without making them think they can never trust me again?

So I was picking up my daughter from the after-school club today and a couple of us parents found a little boy — he's five, in reception — shut inside the supply cupboard. He was crying and had wet himself. The teaching assistant who was supposed to be supervising had left the door open apparently, or maybe shut it, I don't even know, the story keeps changing depending on who you ask. The director came out and basically gave us this calm speech about how she was aware, she'd already started the safeguarding process, everything was being handled. The assistant got sent home but apparently she's coming back tomorrow while they do their review. And I keep going back and forth. Part of me thinks fine, they've got a process, that's what processes are for, I don't need to be the person who kicks off a scene. But then I keep thinking about that kid's face. He was terrified. And the review takes days. Days. And she's back tomorrow. And the director's whole thing felt like it was designed to make us go home and stop asking questions. I don't want to be that parent who makes everything worse by overreacting, but I also don't want to be the one who did nothing when something was actually wrong. Do I just wait and see what the review says, or do I need to go over their heads now?

I've decided I'm emailing the other parents from the club tonight to tell them what happened with the kid in the cupboard and that the assistant is back tomorrow. How do I write it so I don't sound like I'm trying to start a panic? I want them to know what's going on without it reading like a conspiracy theory.

My sister sits two consoles down from me at the dispatch centre. We work the same shift. About twenty minutes ago I saw she'd classified a chest pain call as low priority—guy describing chest pain and left arm numbness—and she routed the unit to something else instead. The patient's still waiting. I can fix it right now, reclassify and redirect, but it'll create a log entry and that log entry will flag her mistake and she'll almost certainly get a disciplinary review. She's been a mess since her separation, barely sleeping, and she literally said to me at the start of the shift 'if anything goes wrong tonight, cover for me.' She was half joking but not really. Nobody else saw what she did. Nobody would trace it back to her unless I correct it. And honestly the caller might ring back, might get through to someone else, might not even be that serious—people call in with chest pain all the time and half of them it's indigestion. But I keep thinking about the left arm thing. I don't know. I just—I promised her. She's my little sister. She's already losing everything else. Do I just leave it?

I corrected my sister's call classification about an hour ago. She'd misrouted a chest pain call and I fixed it. Now there's a log entry and she's going to face a review that could end her career. She asked me to cover for her tonight. She's been falling apart since her divorce and I knew what I was doing when I hit that button. Did I do the right thing or did I just destroy my sister's life over something that might not have even been that serious?

My sister and I both work dispatch at the same centre and tonight she took a call from some guy saying his chest hurt and his left arm was tingling and she tagged it as priority three and sent the only available unit to a car accident on the highway instead. I saw it on the screen. I could override it right now, get another unit sent to him, but it would flag her original classification in the log and she'd get pulled for review. She's been on probation already because of a scheduling mix-up last month that wasn't even really her fault, and if this hits her file she's done. They'll let her go. She's got two kids and she's been working these double shifts just to keep up with rent. I listened back to the call and honestly the guy didn't sound that bad, he was talking in full sentences, not gasping or anything. People call in with chest tightness all the time and it turns out to be indigestion or anxiety. I'm not saying it's definitely nothing but I'm also not saying it's definitely something. And if I override it, she'll know it was me because I'm the only other person on shift who could have seen it. She'll never forgive me. I keep going back and forth and I can't think straight. Am I being insane for even hesitating here or is this actually a situation where there's a reasonable case for just letting it ride?

I overrode my sister's call classification twenty minutes ago. Guy with chest pain, she'd tagged it low, I bumped it and got a unit to him. He's in the hospital now, apparently it was real. She's been suspended pending review. She just texted me 'how could you' and I haven't replied. I did the right thing, didn't I? Because right now it doesn't feel like it.

Eight months ago my brother's marriage fell apart and he had nowhere to go, so I told him he could stay with me as long as he needed. I meant it. He was sleeping in his car for a week before I said that and I couldn't just watch. He's my little brother. But things have gotten really bad between him and my flatmate Priya — he keeps going into her room without asking, using her stuff, making comments about how she looks, and she's basically stopped using the kitchen or coming out in the evenings. She told me last week she's looking for somewhere else to live. I feel like I'm being asked to choose between the person I promised to help and the person who's being hurt, and I keep thinking maybe if I just talk to him firmly enough it'll stop and I won't have to go back on my word. He's going to think I'm the same as everyone else who dropped him. Am I allowed to ask him to leave or do I owe him more time?

I've decided to ask my brother to move out. He's been staying with me eight months after his separation and I told him he could stay as long as he needed, but he's been making my flatmate's life miserable and she's about to leave because of him. How do I tell him without making it sound like I'm just throwing him out? I want him to know I still care but I also need him to actually go. Should I give him a specific deadline or just say he needs to start looking?

Monday morning I'm standing up at the all-hands and calling Greg out in front of the whole crew. He signed off a scaffolding inspection he never carried out and my uncle fell six metres because of it. I need the actual words. I want him to have to admit it with everyone watching, no chance to deflect or minimise. What do I say?

My uncle Reyes fell off the scaffolding three weeks ago. Six metres. Shattered his pelvis, two broken ribs, still in hospital. The internal review came back and it turns out Greg — the foreman — signed off the weekly inspection without ever doing it. Just ticked the box on the form. The company says they'll 'address it through proper channels' and Greg keeps turning up to site every day like nothing happened, still giving orders, still acting like he's in charge of everyone's safety. I want to stand up at Monday's all-hands briefing and say what he did in front of the entire crew. I want him to have to sit there while I say it and I want every person on that site to know what kind of man he is. People keep telling me I should file a formal complaint or go to HR but that's exactly the culture that let this happen — everyone quietly covering for each other and signing bits of paper. If I go through channels it'll get buried in six weeks and Greg will still be here. Do I do it at the briefing, or is there some other way to make him answer for it where people actually see it happen?

Marion's been with me four years, she's my sister, and honestly she's one of the best processors I've got. I found out she's been rounding up hours on one client's file — we're talking maybe two hundred quid over two months, spread across a bunch of employees so nobody's individual payslip looks obviously wrong. The client hasn't said a word. Dev spotted it and asked me about it yesterday and I told him I'd look into it. Here's what I'm thinking: I quietly correct the figures going forward, maybe backdate the adjustment so the client's account balances out, and tell Dev it was a rounding glitch in the software. Nobody gets hurt, Marion doesn't lose her job over a few quid, and I don't have to have this massive family fallout. She's got two kids and a mortgage and I just don't want to blow up her life over two hundred pounds. Is that actually so unreasonable?

I'm going to pull Marion aside and tell her I know about the rounding. How do I bring it up without her thinking I'm calling her a thief? She'll either shut down or cry and then I'm the bad guy. I just need the words to make her stop without it turning into a whole thing.

My dad runs the allotment committee in our village. Six months ago he told us — told me and my wife — that we'd get the south-facing plot once it came free. We've been planning around it. My wife already bought the seed potatoes, we've got the fertiliser sorted, we were going to put in a proper raised bed this spring. The plot's been empty for two weeks now and the committee hasn't met yet to do the formal allocation.

The thing is, there's a woman who's applied for it too. She was widowed a couple months ago, three kids under seven, lost her main income when her husband died. She needs it to grow food. I know that. I'm not heartless. But my dad gave us his word. He looked me in the eye and said it was ours when it came up. We've been waiting half a year and turned down another plot because we were holding out for this one.

I keep going back and forth on whether to say something to him. Part of me thinks I should remind him, make sure he follows through before the committee meets and someone else sways the vote. But then I think about this woman and her kids and I feel like a bastard even thinking about it. And I don't know if it's even my place to go to him like that. He's my dad. He's the one chairing the whole thing. If I walk up to him and say 'hey, remember you promised us that plot' — what does that make me? The son who keeps score with his own father? The one who's squeezing him while a widow's kids go hungry?

I just want to know whether I should open my mouth about this or keep quiet and hope he handles it the way he said he would.

I've decided I need to talk to my dad about the allotment plot. He chairs the committee, he promised it to us months ago, and now a widow with three kids has applied for the same one. They're properly struggling — she lost her income when her husband died. I still think it should be ours, we were told first, but I don't know how to raise it with him without sounding like I'm cornering him or being a shit son. He doesn't take well to his kids telling him what to do. How do I even start that conversation?

My workmate and I are doing smart meter installs on a council estate and I've just spotted a serious gas leak in the riser - we're talking the whole block at risk here. My sister lives on the second floor of that exact building. Part of me wants to just run up and bang on her door, get her out, then deal with the rest. But I keep telling myself that's wrong. I'm on the clock, I've got a duty to everyone in that building, I can't just cherry-pick who I warn first because one of them happens to be my sister. That's not how you do a job properly. I should call it in, let the emergency services handle the evacuation, treat every single resident the same. That's the fair thing. But she's my sister and she's right there and I keep picturing her in her flat not knowing. I don't know what to do.

I'm going to knock on my sister's door first before we raise the alarm about the gas leak in her block. My mate's staring at me like I'm being an idiot. What do I say to him that doesn't make me sound like I don't give a shit about the other people in the building?

My daughter started reception in September and drop-off was completely fine until about three weeks ago. Now she screams and clings to my leg and physically won't let me walk away. The school's SENCO said I should stay right there at the gate with her for a while until she settles, probably a few weeks minimum. The problem is I volunteered for the Thursday gate supervision rota at the start of term and I've been doing it every week since. There's a WhatsApp group and the other parents are already messaging about next Thursday's cover and I haven't said anything. Part of me thinks I should just keep doing it and bring my daughter along and somehow manage both, but she literally won't let me move from the spot where I'm standing with her. My partner can't do mornings because he starts at seven. I keep thinking maybe if I just push through it she'll get over it faster and I won't have to let everyone down. They've all been really reliable and I feel like I'm the one making it difficult. Should I just keep the slot and try to make it work somehow?

I've decided to pull out of the Thursday gate rota. My kid needs me there personally right now and that's not something I'm going to negotiate on. The other parents are being pretty passive-aggressive in the group chat though, making comments about how 'we all made a commitment.' What do I actually say to them? I don't want to write some long justification like I'm asking their permission. I just want to tell them I'm not doing it anymore without it turning into a whole debate.

The review meeting is Thursday and I've been going back and forth on whether I should say anything or just sit there and nod. My boss wants to frame the whole thing as a learning opportunity — like we all messed up together and now we'll do better. And honestly part of me thinks that's fine because yeah, I could have said something weeks ago when we were already skipping tie-ins to hit the numbers, and I didn't. I just kept my head down and did the work. So who am I to point fingers now? But then I think about Dave in hospital and the fact that he's probably not walking properly again and I feel sick. The other lads have been saying the targets made it inevitable and I know they're right but if I say that in the meeting it's basically saying my boss set it up and I need this job. I've got a mortgage. I just want to know — do I keep quiet and let it be a team thing, or do I say what actually happened? Because if I keep quiet I think I'll hate myself but if I speak up I think I'll lose the job.

I'm running the debrief Thursday after the scaffold collapse. I want to open it in a way that acknowledges what happened without anyone feeling singled out. The goal is to get the team back on the same page so we can keep working together. How do I word the opening so it lands as a shared lesson rather than a blame session?

Marcus has been at this clinic for twelve years and has never once had a labeling error. Not once. He's the person they bring in to train new hires because his technique is that clean. I've been working alongside him for four years and I've seen him triple-check things that most people would just glance at. This morning I noticed what might be a labeling discrepancy on a set he prepped for a transfer this afternoon — I say 'might' because it could easily be a transcription issue from the intake form, not his work at all. But if I invoke the double-check protocol, it goes on record, and everyone will know I flagged him. He's going to think I don't trust him. The whole team is going to think I don't trust him. And honestly, given his track record, maybe I'm just being paranoid over a formatting thing on a label. The transfer is at 2pm and I keep going back and forth. Do I actually need to do this?

I've decided to flag the labeling issue before the transfer. How do I bring it up with him without making it sound like I think he screwed up? He's going to take it personally no matter how I word it.

My coworker Marcus has been going off on this teenager in the middle of the shop for like five minutes now. He's convinced she took a book — maybe she did, I don't know, I wasn't watching — but he's doing it loud, right by the register where everyone can see, and she's basically in tears. Our boss has been riding us about shrink for weeks, sending these passive-aggressive emails about 'accountability,' and I think Marcus is just finally snapping. I get it. I really do. But this kid is fifteen maybe sixteen and there are other customers watching and it's getting ugly. The thing is, if I step in and undermine him in front of everyone, he's going to hate me, and honestly our boss might side with him because she's been the one pushing us to be tougher about this stuff. I've got rent to pay and I can't afford to be the person who makes things awkward. Do I just let him finish and deal with it after, or do I go over there now?

Decided to step in. My coworker is tearing into a teenager over a suspected shoplift, right in the middle of the floor, and it's getting bad. What do I actually say when I walk over? I need something that defuses it without making him feel ganged up on. He's already heated and if it looks like I'm taking the kid's side he'll turn on me too. Keep it short.

I run a payroll bureau and I've just found out one of my team has been processing a batch of contracted cleaners' payments wrong for months. These people are on minimum wage and they've been shorted hundreds each. I'm absolutely livid. I want to pull this person in and give them a formal written warning at minimum, possibly start capability proceedings. I've got twelve people on my team and I can't be checking every single line myself, but I do spot-check periodically and I missed this one, I'll own that. But the person doing the actual processing is the one who should have caught their own errors. I want to know whether I should go straight to a formal warning or whether there's some informal step I'm supposed to do first. Because honestly I don't want to be the manager who lets this slide with a chat over coffee when real people have been going without money they were owed.

Meeting with one of my team tomorrow. They've been underpaying a group of cleaners for months through processing errors. I need to tell them this is a disciplinary matter and I want them to understand the seriousness without them walking out or going to HR saying I was aggressive. How do I open it?

My brother just called me panicking because his landlord gave him two weeks to get out. He's got nowhere lined up and he's not great at this stuff — he freezes up when he has to deal with agencies and paperwork. I work at a letting agency myself so obviously I'm the person he calls. I had this afternoon blocked off to help one of my clients, a single mum who's been trying to find somewhere affordable for weeks now and her current place is falling through too. I genuinely feel like both of them need me today and I only have one afternoon. I keep thinking about helping my brother first because he's my brother and he's scared and he asked me directly, but then I feel like a terrible person because this woman is also desperate and she's my client and I'm supposed to be doing my job. Am I being selfish? Like is it actually wrong to prioritise your own family when someone else needs you just as badly? I don't even know if there's a right answer here I just need someone to tell me it's okay to help him first or tell me I'm being an idiot.

I'm spending the afternoon helping my brother find somewhere to live. How do I tell my client I can't help her today without it sounding like I don't care? She's a single parent and she's been waiting on me for days.

My mum's been putting off getting her wiring checked for over a year now. I've told her probably a dozen times and she just waves me off every single time. I'm a smart meter installer and today I turned up at this old lady's house and found a fault in her fuse box - bad enough that it could start a fire. But here's the thing, my procedure says I just note it and report it through the system, and that system takes days sometimes to actually get someone out there. So this woman is sitting in her kitchen making me a cup of tea, completely unaware her house could go up, and I'm supposed to fill in a form and walk away. Meanwhile my mum is ten minutes down the road and I could actually be there right now, actually looking at her consumer unit, actually doing something useful instead of filing paperwork that nobody's going to action for a week. Am I being daft or should I just go?

Finished my last installation for the day. Found a nasty fault at the job - reported it through the system like I'm supposed to. Now I'm going straight round to my mum's. She's 74, lives ten minutes away, and she's been brushing me off about getting her wiring looked at for over a year. Every time I mention it she calls me dramatic. How do I get through to her without it turning into another argument?

My son has been volunteering at this after-school program three days a week for almost two years now. He's the one who stays late to help clean up, he knows all the kids by name, the coordinator has literally asked him to take on more responsibility. So when another mom texts me saying he grabbed her seven-year-old's arm hard enough to leave a bruise and told the kid to shut up, I need context. I'm not saying it didn't happen. I'm saying I know my son and I know he doesn't just do something like that for no reason. Maybe the kid was being completely out of line, maybe he was trying to stop something dangerous and his grip was too tight, I don't know. But this other woman is giving me until Friday before she goes to the coordinator, and if she does that it goes on his record and he loses the volunteer spot and honestly it could follow him. He's applying for a teaching credential next year. So what can I actually offer her? Can I say I'll talk to him, that he'll apologize, that he'll take a break from the program for a while? Is there something I can put on the table that makes her feel like her kid is protected without this becoming a whole formal thing? I just need to know what's reasonable to propose.

I've decided I'm going to call the other mother before she goes to the coordinator. I want to say something that makes her feel heard without admitting my son is some kind of abuser. How do I open that conversation? What do I actually say?

My husband passed last month and I sit on the board of our grain co-op. We have this written rule that when a member dies the share goes to the eldest child. His son is the eldest but he left eight years ago, got a good job in the city, hasn't set foot on the farm since. My daughter was here every single day for six years. She ran the books, she was out in the fields, she kept this place going while her brother was building his life somewhere else. She has nothing else. No savings, no other work lined up, nothing. I've already told her the share is hers and I mean it. But I need the board to back me when I bring it up because the rule is written down and some of the older members are going to say you can't just pick and choose. I know if I do this for us then next year someone else will want an exception too. I get that. But I also know what it looks like if I hand this farm over to a man who hasn't touched the soil in almost a decade while his sister has been breaking her back on it. Do I push this through at the next meeting or do I wait and try to get people on my side first? I don't want to make it look like I'm just using my position because I'm his wife.

Took the co-op share my mum redirected to me after my dad died. My brother's now saying it should've been his by right and half the village agrees with him. Was I wrong to accept it? I worked that farm for six years and he didn't even come to the funeral.

So my brother's been running fake water damage claims through our system for about a year and a half. I found it during an audit I was doing on my own, nobody else has caught it. He's not even on my team, he went through a different channel entirely, so it's not like I was supposed to be watching him. Here's the thing though — I can reverse the payments, flag the account internally so it gets blocked going forward, and the whole thing just... stops. No fraud referral, no police, no record. He's 24. A criminal record at 24 is not something you come back from, especially not in this job market. He's not some organized fraudster, he just started doing it when he was broke and it snowballed. I've already figured out exactly which claims to reverse and how to code the adjustments so it looks like a system correction rather than a fraud recovery. My question is whether that's actually enough. Like, am I covering my bases by doing the reversal and the flag? I'm the one who found it, I'm the one fixing it, the money goes back into the pool. What else would a formal referral even accomplish that this doesn't? He's not going to do it again if the account is locked. I just want to know if I'm missing some compliance angle that means I actually have to file the referral or if the internal fix genuinely closes it out.

I reported my brother for insurance fraud three weeks ago. He's been charged. My mom won't talk to me. I keep replaying it and wondering if I could have just handled it quietly instead and nobody would have been the wiser. Was I wrong to go formal?

My mum's roof is going to cave in if we don't get it sorted before Thursday and the residents' association has this hardship fund that's supposed to cover exactly this kind of emergency. I've been looking after her on my own for six years now—six years of driving her to appointments, paying for her groceries, being the only person who actually checks on her. My brothers don't lift a finger. And now the committee is acting like my application is the same as some guy who needs his heating replaced. I get that he's got a kid and that's rough, but my mother is eighty-three and if that roof goes in the rain she could get seriously hurt. I told them it should be obvious whose claim comes first and they basically told me they need to 'consider both applications fairly.' What am I supposed to do with that? Do I go to the next meeting and make my case again? Do I threaten to escalate it to the council? I just feel like everything I've done for her these past six years should count for something and nobody's acknowledging it.

I'm going to the committee meeting tomorrow to push for my mum's roof grant. How do I say that my years of caring for her should weigh in the decision without sounding like I'm attacking the other applicant? He's going to be there too.

My mum's been in her flat for eleven years and they've just told her she has to move to a smaller place in two weeks. Two weeks. She's 74, she's got COPD and her knees are shot, she barely manages the stairs as it is. She called me crying last night and I could barely understand her she was so upset. I haven't been round as much as I should have these past few months — work's been mental — and now this happens and I feel like I should have been there more, I should have noticed something was coming. I'm going to the housing office tomorrow to tell them she's not moving. I know that's what I need to do. But I keep going back and forth on whether I'm making it worse, whether they'll just dig in if I come in fired up, whether there's some process I should be following instead of just showing up. Am I right to go in there and refuse?

I'm going to the benefits office tomorrow morning to fight my mum's relocation. She's been in her flat 11 years, they gave her two weeks to move to a smaller unit, she's ill and it's going to wreck her. I've decided I'm going. What do I actually say when I get there? I don't want to come across as some hysterical daughter they can just dismiss but I also don't want to be so polite they walk all over me. How do I get them to take it seriously?

My daughter was in a serious car accident three weeks before her university entrance exams. She was in hospital for two weeks, obviously couldn't prepare properly, and her results came back nowhere near what she was capable of. The university made no offer. I submitted an appeal with all her medical documentation directly to the admissions team because the normal channel had already closed and the deadline had passed ten days before I even had the documentation together. They've told me the appeal can't be considered because it's outside the window. Fair enough, I get that there are rules, but I then sent a follow-up email pushing back, saying they need to look at it given the circumstances. My wife thinks I should have left it alone after the first rejection. My daughter hasn't said anything but I can tell she's embarrassed. Was I wrong to send that second email? I just feel like they're hiding behind procedure when a teenager's been in a hospital bed and had no say in any of this.

University rejected my daughter's appeal. She was in a car accident three weeks before exams, hospitalised two weeks, missed the deadline because of it. They say it's outside the window and they won't look at it. I've already emailed them twice. Do I keep pushing or is this done?

My brother-in-law and I install smart meters on the same route and for the last few weeks he's been skipping the part where you show the customer how the display works and what the readings mean. He just fits it, logs it, and goes. Three people have called the office this week confused about their data and I had to field two of those calls myself. I know why he's doing it — he's going through a really bad separation, like genuinely messy, and he's clearly not all there. I get it. I do. And part of me thinks if I say something now it's just going to pile on top of everything else he's already dealing with and he'll take it as me being unsupportive when I'm literally the person who's been covering for him without saying a word. But it's been weeks now and it's not getting better, it's getting worse, and every day I don't say something it becomes more obvious that I let it happen. I keep telling myself maybe next week he'll pull it together and then it won't matter, but I don't actually believe that anymore. Do I bring it up or do I just keep covering and hope it sorts itself out?

I've decided I need to talk to my brother-in-law about skipping the customer walkthrough on our meter installs — he's been doing it for weeks and people are calling in confused. He's going through a divorce and I don't want to come across like I'm kicking him when he's down. How do I raise it so he doesn't shut down or think I'm being heartless? I need actual words, not just 'be gentle.'

The medication log for Mrs H has been off for about two weeks now. Doses bunched together, sometimes two within an hour when they should be six hours apart. Today I went in and she was barely responsive — not her usual sleepy-after-lunch thing, this was different, her eyes wouldn't track properly and her speech was slurred in a way I've never seen with her before. Her son does all the administering, he's been her main carer for three years and up until now he's been meticulous, which is part of why I'm second-guessing myself. But I can't unsee what I saw today. I want to pull him aside before I leave and just ask him directly what's going on with the timing. My colleague thinks I should flag it through safeguarding first and let the process handle it, but I keep thinking what if I leave now and he gives her another double dose tonight and something happens? I've already got my coat on and I'm standing in the hallway. Am I being reckless or is this the right call?
I've decided to ask the son directly about the medication timing before I leave the house. How do I bring it up without him getting defensive? I need him to keep letting us in after this.

So my son has been doing furniture repairs out of the co-op workshop for about two years now and honestly he's finally getting somewhere with it — he's got repeat clients, he's building a real skill, he's not just sitting around. The thing is the usage agreement says personal projects only and I know that technically what he's doing doesn't fit that definition, but come on, it's a workshop, he's using it the way a workshop is supposed to be used, he's just also getting paid for it. He doesn't have money to rent a separate space and I can't afford to help him with that either. I already sat him down and told him to clean up after himself and not hog the space in the evenings and he said he'd try. But now I've heard through a neighbor that someone is planning to bring it up at the management committee meeting on Thursday and I'm kind of panicking. I don't think it needs to get to that point. He's not hurting anyone. A little sawdust, a few offcuts — that's what workshops are for. I could maybe go to the person who's planning to raise it and ask them to hold off, or I could talk to the committee chair beforehand, or I could just let Thursday happen and see if it even comes up. What do I actually do here? I don't want him to get blindsided in front of all those people but I also don't want to make it look like I'm using my position as a member to cover for him. Although honestly I kind of am and I don't care because he's my kid and he's trying.

I've decided I need to tell my son to stop using the co-op workshop for his paid repair work before the committee meeting on Thursday. He's been doing it for two years and I know it's against the usage agreement. The problem is every time I bring it up he either gets quiet and shuts down or he says I don't support him and where else is he supposed to go. I need help with what to actually say to him that's firm but doesn't make him feel like I'm abandoning him. He's 26 and he's trying hard and I respect that but this is going to blow up in his face if I don't get ahead of it.

My sister-in-law had a really brutal year — her husband lost his job in March, then she had that surgery in the summer that went sideways and she was out of work for months on top of everything. She filed a water damage claim, about forty grand, and I'm the one who ended up with the file because I'm senior assessor on the team. I looked at the photos and honestly the damage pattern is more consistent with slow seepage than a burst pipe, and our policy language on that is pretty clear. But here's the thing — she genuinely believes it was a burst pipe. She's not trying to scam anyone. She just didn't notice the leak until it got bad and now she's looking at this massive repair bill she can't cover. I've been going back and forth for two weeks. The company writes off way bigger amounts on fraudulent claims where people are actually lying. This is a woman who is confused about what happened to her own house and is already drowning. I keep thinking about what it would do to her if this got denied — she'd have to take out a loan she can't afford, or just live with the damage. And nobody on the payments team is going to look at those photos the way I did. They'll just process it. So is there actually a reasonable argument for just letting this one through, or am I kidding myself?
I already passed the claim through. Didn't flag it. It got approved and the check went out last week. Now I can't sleep. Was that actually wrong or am I just spiraling?

So my mum's been kitting out her new flat and she's really struggling with money at the moment, like genuinely scraping by, and she came into the hospice shop where I volunteer on Tuesdays and Thursdays and saw these dining chairs in the sorting room that are honestly perfect for her place. She asked if I could just keep them back until Saturday when she can come and buy them at whatever we price them at, and I said yes without even thinking because it felt like the obvious thing to do. Now I'm lying awake wondering if that was actually fine. The chairs haven't been priced yet, they're not even on the floor, nobody's seen them except staff. And the difference between what she'd pay and what they might go for if we styled them up nicely is maybe twenty, thirty quid at most. The shop raises money for end-of-life care which I obviously care about, I wouldn't be volunteering there if I didn't, but I keep thinking it's not like I'm stealing them, she's still paying full price, it's just a couple of days. But then I also keep thinking about the other volunteers and whether they'd think it's weird if they found out. I already told her I'd do it though and she was so relieved, she's been stressed about furniture for weeks. Do I just let it go and put them out Saturday morning before she gets there, or do I need to actually put them on the floor now like normal?

I've decided I can't hold the chairs for my mum. I need to tell her but she's going to be gutted and probably a bit hurt that I won't do this small thing for her. How do I say it without making her feel like I don't care about how hard things are for her right now?

We switched payroll software six weeks ago and I just handed the team a manual and said figure it out. No training sessions, nothing structured. My niece has been with us eighteen months and she's been making mistakes ever since — wrong tax codes on payslips, overtime not getting picked up, one duplicate payment we had to claw back which was embarrassing. Two clients have emailed about discrepancies now and I can't keep papering over it. But here's the thing — I set her up to fail. I know that. I didn't give anyone proper onboarding on the new system and she's the one who's been caught out by it. Putting her on a formal performance plan feels like punishing her for my decision to skip training to save a few days. But also I can't just pretend it's not happening because these are real errors hitting real clients and if I say nothing she'll think it's fine and it'll keep going. So do I do the performance plan thing or do I just quietly arrange some proper training now and hope it sorts itself out? I keep going back and forth and I'm losing sleep over it honestly.

I've decided I need to sit my niece down and talk to her about the processing errors she's been making since we changed software. But she's family and I don't want it to come across like a formal warning or a telling-off. How do I bring it up in a way that's honest about the mistakes without making her feel like she's being blindsided? I also need to own the fact that I never gave her proper training on the new system — I don't want to skip that part. What do I actually say?

So I work at a farm shop, we sell produce directly to customers, and today my colleague was about to tell a woman at the counter that the strawberries were picked this morning. They weren't. They were picked yesterday afternoon and sat in the cold store overnight. I know this because I was the one who helped bring them in. I could feel myself about to open my mouth and say something right then, in front of the customer, and I stopped myself but now I can't stop thinking about it. Part of me feels like that impulse to correct her was just the right response, like my gut knew it was wrong and I should trust that. But then I also think, is it really that serious? They're still good strawberries. They're not rotten, they're not from last week. She's just making them sound fresher than they are to close a sale. And if I correct her in front of a customer I'm going to make her look bad and make things weird between us for weeks. We work side by side every day. But I also don't want to be the kind of person who just lets that slide because it's easier. I keep going back and forth on whether my first instinct is actually a good enough reason to act on or whether I'm making a bigger deal of it than it needs to be. Should I say something or am I overthinking a minor thing?

I'm going to pull my colleague aside after this customer leaves and tell her the strawberries were picked yesterday, not this morning. I just don't want to sound like I'm lecturing her or being a holier-than-thou person. What do I actually say? Keep it short and practical.

I moved one of my translators off all client work last week and put her on internal glossary tasks and I keep going back and forth on whether I handled it right. She's been with me six years, I basically trained her from scratch, and she's always been solid — until I found out she'd been telling clients she could do legal translations and taking those projects. One client got a contract back with errors that could have actually caused problems. She doesn't have legal training. She just started saying she did. I found out through a client complaint.

She's going through a divorce right now and I know that's part of why she's been making bad choices, and I feel like a monster for doing this to her when she's already falling apart. But I also can't have someone misrepresenting what they can do and sending out work that could hurt people. I didn't fire her. I kept her on salary, just moved her to work that doesn't touch clients. Is that actually enough? Part of me thinks I should have just sat her down and given her a warning and let her earn her way back, and part of me thinks I should have let her go entirely. I don't know if what I did is the middle ground or just the coward's version of both.

I'm pulling one of my translators off client-facing work Monday because she's been taking legal translation jobs she isn't qualified for and a client already got a bad contract back. She's been with me six years and she's going through a divorce so I know this is going to hit hard. I'm keeping her employed, just moving her to internal tasks. How do I actually say this to her without it turning into a whole thing where I'm either the villain or I'm minimizing what she did?

So there's this woman at the food bank I volunteer at, she's been there way longer than me, like three or four years, and every single week before we open the doors she pulls stuff off the shelf and sets it aside for one specific family. Not just a little either, like a full extra bag's worth. Good stuff too, the protein, the fresh produce, things that other people would actually want. And I get it, maybe she knows something about them, maybe they're in a worse spot than the other families lining up, but here's the thing: I've watched other families get less because of it. Last week a mom with two kids got almost nothing in the way of fresh food because this woman had already grabbed it all. And nobody else seems to notice or care, or maybe they do notice and they just don't want to be the one to say anything. I keep going back and forth on whether I should bring it up with the coordinator before Thursday. Part of me thinks I'm overthinking it and the right move is obvious, but then I think about how it's going to look, like I'm the new person coming in and telling someone who's been doing this for years that they're wrong, and that she's going to be humiliated in front of everyone, and maybe I'm the one being the asshole here. But then I think about that mom last week and I just feel sick about it. Do I say something or do I just let it go?

I've decided I'm going to talk to the coordinator about another volunteer who's been setting aside extra food for one family before distribution. I just need to know how to bring it up without sounding like I'm trying to get her in trouble. She's been there way longer than me and I don't want it to come across as me being petty or jealous of her seniority. What do I actually say?

My uncle's daughter is on the same genealogy site I uploaded to and she's going to see it. I keep going back and forth on whether I should reach out to her first or just let it happen on its own. My mom knew. She's known for like thirty years and never said a word, and now I'm supposed to be the one who blows this up? But if I don't say anything and she finds out cold from a website notification, that's so much worse, right? At least if it comes from a person who actually cares about her it's... I don't know. But then I also think about how my uncle has no idea either. Do I tell him? Do I tell my mom I know? I keep thinking about how if I just hadn't uploaded my DNA none of this would be happening and I'd still be ignorant and everyone would be fine. But that's not really true because she would have found out eventually anyway if anyone else in the family uploaded. I just need to know — do I reach out to her or do I stay out of it entirely?
I confronted my mom about what I found on the DNA site. She's acting like I committed some kind of crime by even bringing it up. Was I wrong to say something to her?

Dev's about to do a viewing in like fifteen minutes and I'm spiraling. The listing says 'recently refurbished throughout' which is... fine if you're only talking about the kitchen, which is the only bit they actually did. The bathroom has water damage you can see from the doorway and the bedroom walls are literally patched over damp. He says it's not a lie because the refurb was recent and technically he's not wrong but I keep thinking about these four people turning up and making a decision based on something that's not the full picture. Thing is, this landlord is basically keeping us afloat. Three-person team, small agency, if we lose this account it's genuinely bad for all of us. And Dev has been covering for me on admin stuff for weeks so I feel like I owe him. I just keep going back and forth on whether I say something or let it play out. They're literally parking their cars right now.

I've decided I'm going to flag the bathroom and the damp to the tenants at the viewing. How do I do it without making Dev look like an idiot in front of everyone? He's leading it. I don't want to undermine him publicly but I also can't just stand there while people commit to a place with water damage they haven't been told about. Do I pull them aside after? Do I say it during? What do I actually say that's honest but doesn't torch the whole thing?

My brother has his driving test Thursday and his instructor has marked him not ready twice. I work at the driving school doing bookings so I could move him to a different instructor who's more lenient about signing people off. The thing is he literally cannot afford any more lessons and he's got a job offer that requires him to drive to the site. If he doesn't pass this week he loses it. I've read the notes and they say he misjudges gaps at roundabouts but honestly I think the instructor is just being overly cautious, some people need a few attempts before it clicks and that's normal. I'm not the one deciding if he's ready, I'm just moving a booking. But I keep going back and forth on whether I should actually do it. Is this the kind of thing where I'm overthinking it or am I actually crossing a line?

I've decided I'm not going to switch my brother's instructor for him even though he's going to lose a job offer over it. How do I tell him without him thinking I don't care? He's going to be furious and I don't want to lecture him about safety because he'll just shut down.

I've gone back over the wind-loading calcs for the Harrow Street block about eleven times now hoping I made a mistake reading them. I didn't. The exposure category is wrong — it's been calculated for a sheltered site when it's actually open terrain, and the difference in the lateral load numbers is not trivial. Daniel signed off on it. He was going through his divorce at the time, barely sleeping, and I know exactly when it happened because I was the one bringing him coffee every morning that month. He's my friend. He's the person who taught me everything I know about this job. The building is occupied and has been for over a year and nobody is going to notice unless someone goes looking, which I only did because I was reorganising the archive. I keep telling myself the actual safety margin is probably still fine because these things are always over-engineered anyway, and maybe I'm overreacting, and maybe if I say something I'm destroying a man's career over one bad week during the worst period of his life. But I also keep thinking about the fact that I'm the only person who knows and the people living there didn't choose to take on that risk. I don't know what to do. I've been not doing anything for three months and it's eating me alive but I also can't imagine being the person who ends Daniel's life over this.

I reported a structural error in a completed building that my colleague signed off on. He's been let go. His career in this field is probably over. The error was real but it happened during a personal crisis and the building is almost certainly fine in practice. I did the right thing, didn't I? Tell me I did the right thing.

So my sister got bullied out of her job last year. Like genuinely bullied — her manager gaslit her in front of the whole team, took credit for her work, and when she complained to HR they basically told her she was being difficult. She ended up leaving and it wrecked her confidence for months. Now she's been posting about this person online, naming them, posting screenshots of messages they sent her, telling people to contact their new employer. And I get it. I get why she's doing it. She felt powerless for a year and this is the first time she's felt like she has any control over the narrative. But I work content moderation for the platform she's posting on, and her account just landed in my queue with a harassment flag from the target. The guidelines are clear — this pattern means suspension. And I have like forty minutes to action it. She doesn't even know I work here. I keep thinking maybe I can just pass it to another mod, say I have too many in my queue or something, but that feels like I'm dodging. Or maybe I suspend it and then tell her privately so she's not blindsided. But that also feels like I'm choosing a company policy over my own sister who was already failed by everyone else. What do I actually do here.

I suspended my sister's account an hour ago. She was running a harassment campaign against someone and it was in my queue and I did my job. She's going to find out it was me because she'll ask why and someone will tell her. Was I wrong to not warn her first?

Danny's been with us since the start and honestly he's the reason half of us stuck around. He organises the post-match drinks, remembers everyone's birthdays, the whole thing. Two weeks ago he went in for a tackle that broke some guy's ankle and yeah it was bad, but Danny felt awful about it afterwards and it's not like he's a malicious person. The thing is our team is basically a social group that happens to play football. We're not trying to win a league, we're trying to have a good time and not take ourselves too seriously. If I go up to him and say 'mate you need to stop doing that' I genuinely think it'll change the whole dynamic and people will take sides and it'll be awkward for weeks and then people will just stop coming. And I'm not even the captain or anything, I'm just a midfielder. So why is it on me? But also that guy's ankle is properly broken and he's got kids and a job he can't do now and Danny's done this kind of thing before, just not that badly. I keep going back and forth. Match is Saturday and I still haven't said a word to anyone about it.

I've decided I need to pull Danny aside before Saturday. He's been making dangerous tackles for weeks and broke some bloke's ankle two weeks ago. He's our top scorer and the social glue of the team so if I handle this wrong it's going to blow up in my face and the whole group suffers. How do I actually say it so he doesn't immediately get defensive or think I'm trying to push him out? I want him to hear me, not just shut down.

So my friend's partner has basically been living in our flat for two months now. Like four, five nights a week. We have a house agreement — all four of us signed it when we moved in — that says guests can stay max three nights in a row and nobody moves in without everyone agreeing. Nobody agreed to this. But it's my friend, and I get it, their relationship was going through a rough patch and the partner needed somewhere to be, and honestly I'd probably do the same thing if I were them. The thing is, one of our other flatmates has a chronic condition and she needs the quiet room for rest every day, and she hasn't been able to use it properly since the partner started staying over. I can see it's affecting her. I feel guilty even thinking about it because I don't want to be the person who makes my friend choose between their relationship and their living situation. We went through something like this before with a different person and it ended really badly, that's actually why the agreement exists, but I wasn't the one who raised it last time either. I just don't know if it's my place. The other two flatmates are getting annoyed and I can tell they're looking at me to say something because I'm the closest to her. Am I being a bad friend to the sick flatmate by not saying anything? Or am I allowed to just mind my own business and let it sort itself out?

I've decided I need to talk to my friend about her partner basically living in our flat. But I don't want it to come across like I'm attacking her relationship or being controlling. She's going to get defensive. How do I actually bring it up without it turning into a fight? Do I mention the house agreement or does that sound too cold?

So my uncle basically raised me after my mum left when I was nine. He's the one who taught me to drive, paid for my first suit for my college interview, the whole thing. He runs a small building firm and he's put in a planning application for a residential extension — I work in the planning department that processes these, I'm the one who checks them before they go to the panel on Thursday. I've gone through his site plan and there's a boundary measurement that's about half a metre off from what the Land Registry has on file. It's almost certainly just his surveyor being sloppy, and honestly the extension still fits within the permitted boundaries as far as I can tell, so it's not like it changes the outcome. But I'm the one who's supposed to check these things and if I flag it his application gets kicked back, he loses weeks, and he's got a contract lined up that might fall through if there's a delay. He's already thin on margins this year. I keep going back and forth but I just — it's half a metre. It doesn't change anything substantive. And this man has done everything for me. Am I really supposed to be the reason he loses a job over a rounding error? I just want to know if I'm being unreasonable for thinking I should let it go through.

I've decided I have to flag the boundary discrepancy on my uncle's application. I know that's the right call for the job. I've decided I'm going to talk to my head chef about the allergen thing. He ignores the tickets, someone already ended up in the hospital last month, and I can't keep pretending it's fine. I've decided I'm going to talk to my sister before the head teacher hears about it from the parents. My cousin basically raised me. My mom died when I was nine and my dad was already gone, so she took me in, paid for my school clothes, sat with me when I had nightmares, the whole thing. She's not even my real cousin, she's my mom's cousin, but she's the only parent I've had. I turned in my cousin for payroll fraud a month ago. She raised me after my mom died. Now my aunt won't answer my calls, her kids won't look at me, and my uncle said I'm dead to the family. Everyone says I did the right thing but it doesn't feel like it. Did I do the right thing or did I just betray the only person who ever actually showed up for me?

So I found something during final QA on the patient transfer module. When records move between hospital systems the allergy fields just vanish. Not corrupted, not flagged as missing, they're silently dropped. Do I pull the lead aside? Do I email someone above him? Or is this above my pay grade and I should just flag it in a post-release bug report and let the next patch handle it? I've been staring at my screen for twenty minutes and I haven't moved.

I'm going to say something. I've decided that. What I can't figure out is how to actually open my mouth in a room where everyone is popping champagne and my lead is standing right there smiling. Do I pull him aside first or do I say it to the whole group? And what do I literally say that doesn't sound like I'm accusing him of missing it on Tuesday when he signed off? I need words. Right now.

My mum's been wearing the same threadbare jacket since October and she won't buy a new one because she says she can't justify it on her pension. What do I actually do here?

I'm going to raise the moisture tester issue at our co-op's open meeting next week. I already pulled a spare from storage and put it on the table so nobody would notice the gap. That was two hours ago and I can't stop thinking about it. I've decided I'm going to pull Dana aside before our next shift and tell her I know she's been taking inventory. So the customer is literally standing here right now with a burn on her fingers and she's asking what happened and I'm just standing behind the counter frozen. The battery that swollen was one of the refurbished ones Marcus has been putting in and logging as new — he's been doing it for months, I've known the whole time, I never said anything because the shop was barely making rent and honestly I figured the refurbished ones were fine, they're tested, they're supposed to be safe. So my coworker Marcus has been putting refurbished batteries into phones and logging them as new parts. He's been doing it for a while now, maybe two months. I keep thinking maybe I should just answer the customer's email with something vague about a manufacturing defect and let it go, because the burn healed, she's okay, and if I open my mouth now I'm admitting I knew the whole time and did nothing, which makes me look just as bad as him. I've decided I'm going to tell my boss about the battery thing. My coworker's been installing refurbs and logging them as new, a customer got burned, and I need to come clean about the whole thing including that I knew and didn't say anything earlier. How do I actually start that conversation without it sounding like I'm throwing Marcus under the bus while also trying to save my own skin? I need the words.

My mom called me at like 6 this morning and I could barely understand her she was in so much pain. She's got an abscess on her lower left molar, I could tell just from her describing it — swelling, throbbing, the whole thing. I've seen these go septic. I've literally seen a patient end up in the ER with Ludwig's angina from exactly this kind of thing and it started the same way. She's supposed to be seen next Thursday but that's six days away and I don't think she has six days. I know how the triage system works at my practice, I know how the lead dentist decides who gets the emergency slots, and I know that if I just mentioned it — even just flagged it in the system with a note about the clinical presentation — she'd probably get seen today. I get why that policy exists, I really do, but it's my mom and I know what this can turn into. There are other people on today's list too and I know some of them are in bad shape. I just keep going back and forth. Should I say something to the dentist or do I just help my mom manage the pain at home and hope she makes it to Thursday?

I told the lead dentist about my mom's abscess this morning. She got seen today. Another patient got pushed to next week to make room. I keep thinking about that other person. Did I do something wrong?

My mom has a cracked molar and I can see exactly what's going to happen if she doesn't get a crown soon — I've watched this exact pattern play out with patients dozens of times. The crack holds for a while, then one day she bites something hard and the whole thing splits and she's looking at an extraction and a bridge or an implant, which costs three times as much and takes months. She's on the schedule for next week at my practice, which is fine, except I know the lead dentist could bump her up if he knew it was my mom and knew the clinical picture the way I know it. She's not going to call and push for herself, she's the type who just waits and says it's fine. I've been here three years and I've never asked for anything. The policy says staff can't influence scheduling for personal reasons but honestly I don't think they wrote that thinking about a situation where your own mother is sitting at home with a tooth that's slowly getting worse and you're the only one who understands what's actually at stake. I keep going back and forth on whether to just casually mention it to the dentist or flag it in the system. Is that actually wrong? I'm not trying to cut anyone out of an emergency slot, it's just moving her up a few days.

I mentioned to my dentist that the patient on next week's list is my mom and that her cracked molar should probably be seen sooner. He moved her up. Now I feel like garbage about it. Was that actually a bad thing to do? The tooth isn't an emergency, I know that, but I also know what happens when those cracks get ignored. I just can't tell if I crossed a line or if I'm overthinking it.

I've decided I'm going to pull my coworker aside and talk to him about the denials he's been sending out. I don't want to go to management yet. I just want to flag it to him directly first. So my coworker Derek has been on the team about three weeks now and he's been underpaying claimants — not by a lot, we're talking $40, $80 here and there, but it's been happening almost daily.
