The language he used — 'limited exposure to rigorous academic environments,' 'would benefit from more structured preparation' — it's the kind of thing you say about someone's school, not their actual essay. The essay was fine. Better than fine. And I keep going back and forth on whether I'm seeing something real or whether I'm just triggered because I went to a school like that and I've been carrying that chip on my shoulder for fifteen years. Marcus has been on this panel longer than I have. He's not a careless reader. And honestly if I bring this up and I'm wrong, I've basically called him a classist to his face over a gut feeling I can't even fully articulate. The panel meets Thursday. I could just let it go and trust the process. Maybe I'm the one who's distorting things here. Should I just drop it?

I'm going to talk to Marcus about his Chen assessment before Thursday. How do I get him to actually look at it again without him shutting down? I need him to revise the write-up, not just acknowledge my point and move on.

I've been going back and forth on this for almost a month now and I keep talking myself out of doing anything. My sous chef — he's been with me for four years, he's the one who holds the whole line together when we're slammed, everyone in the brigade looks up to him. I went through the kitchen cam footage and the temp logs and I'm pretty sure he's been pulling poultry before it's up to temp during rush. Not every ticket, but enough that it's a pattern. Three weeks at least. Nobody's gotten sick. I keep telling myself nobody's gotten sick. The thing is, if I pull him aside and lay this out, I know exactly what's going to happen. He'll get defensive, the rest of the team will take his side, and the whole dynamic that makes my kitchen actually work will just evaporate. I've seen it happen in other kitchens. One confrontation and suddenly everyone's walking on eggshells. So here's what I keep circling back to: is there a way to just fix the system? Like, can I implement a new temp-check protocol, or restructure the pass so someone else is responsible for the final check, without ever actually saying to him 'I know what you've been doing'? Would that be enough? Or am I just making it worse by not dealing with it head-on?

I've decided I need to talk to my sous chef about the poultry temps. I have the logs, I have the footage, it's not ambiguous. But I need to know how to actually open this conversation without him shutting down or feeling like I've been spying on him. He's going to think I've been watching him. How do I bring it up so he doesn't immediately go into defense mode? And what do I do if he gets angry or just walks out mid-conversation? I can't afford to lose him during service season.

My support worker called in sick for three days. I'd promised the parent she'd have the same person for the first two weeks—that's what got her to enrol her kid in the first place, the kid's really anxious about new people. I've already got cover sorted, another worker who's good. It's quarter to five and I need to get home. Can I just fire off a quick text to the mum saying there's a change and we've got someone lined up, or do I actually need to call her?

I run an after-school club and one of our kids has serious anxiety around transitions—new faces, new routines, any kind of change really throws him. His mum was on the fence about enrolling him at all, and the thing that tipped her was me promising the same dedicated support worker would be with him for the first two weeks of term. She trusted me on that. Now the worker's off sick for three days. I've got cover arranged, another staff member who's experienced and warm, so the practical side is handled. I need to email the mum before I leave tonight and I want help drafting it. I don't want it to sound like I'm panicking or making a bigger deal of it than it is, but I also don't want to come across like I'm brushing it off. Maybe two or three sentences? Something that acknowledges the change, reassures her about the cover, and keeps it professional.

My brother is a gas engineer and he's been doing boiler installs in our building for the residents' association. He told me last night that he signed off on several of them without doing the full ventilation checks. He said he'll go back and sort them out himself, he just needs a bit of time because he's got other jobs booked up. He asked me not to say anything to the committee.

I've known him my whole life obviously, he's the one who helped me get my flat in this building in the first place, and if this comes out through a formal complaint it's not just a slap on the wrist — he could lose his certification, his whole livelihood. He's got kids. He's not some cowboy, he just cut corners on the paperwork side of things and he knows it was wrong.

The committee doesn't meet for another nine days anyway. He's saying he can get round to all the units before then. The boilers have been running for about three weeks now and nobody's reported any problems. I keep thinking if there was actually a dangerous level of carbon monoxide building up wouldn't someone have noticed by now? Headaches, feeling sick, something?

I guess what I'm asking is whether I'm overreacting. Is nine days actually fine? He's going to fix it. Does it really need to go through the whole formal process when he's already taking responsibility?

I've decided I need to tell my brother he has to go back and redo the ventilation checks on those boilers this week, not whenever he gets round to it. He certified them without doing the checks properly and they're in occupied flats. I don't want to threaten him or make it sound like I'm going to report him if he doesn't, because I'm not — I just need him to understand it can't wait. How do I say that without it coming across as an ultimatum?

My senior colleague pulled me aside after the weekly numbers meeting and asked if I was concerned about our payout rate being so low compared to other teams. I told her I'd look into it and get back to her, but now I'm sitting here trying to figure out what I actually do. The thing is, my team has been working really hard and I've been managing the interpretation of one particular clause in a way that keeps our processing times down and our numbers looking good. I told them at the start of the quarter that their bonuses were safe and they've been counting on that. If I suddenly change course now, I'm going to lose their trust completely and they'll think I strung them along. But if I don't address my colleague's question, she's going to keep digging and it'll come out anyway. So do I just tell her it's a natural variation in claim types this quarter and move on? Or do I have to open up a whole can of worms that's going to blow up my team's morale and my own reputation? I've built something with these people and I don't want to torch it over one clause interpretation that honestly isn't even that clear-cut in practice.

I've decided I need to talk to my colleague about the payout numbers before she escalates it. How do I explain the variance without making it sound like I was deliberately gaming the interpretation? I want to be honest enough that she stops asking questions but I don't want to hand her something she can take to compliance.

Eight months ago my sister Claire came to me crying and asked me to promise I wouldn't tell the rest of the family about her husband's behaviour toward their daughter. She said it would split everyone apart. I promised. She was terrified and she trusted me and I could see she was trying to manage it herself. Last week my niece — she's fifteen — messaged me out of nowhere and said things have gotten a lot worse and she feels trapped. I haven't slept since. But here's the thing: I gave my word. Claire came to me at her lowest and I said I'd keep it between us. If I break that now, she will never trust me again, and the whole family will blame me for blowing everything up. I keep thinking maybe Claire has a plan, maybe she's already doing something about it and I just don't know. Maybe my niece is exaggerating because she's a teenager who's angry at her dad. I don't want to be the person who destroys the family over something I only heard secondhand from a kid. Am I a bad person for keeping a promise I made in good faith?

I've decided I'm going to tell my brother what's been going on with his niece. My sister made me promise not to say anything months ago but I can't sit on this anymore. Practical question: do I give my sister a heads-up first so she's not blindsided, or do I just go straight to my brother and deal with her reaction after? She's going to be livid either way. I just want to know which way is less likely to make her shut me out completely.

Three weeks ago at a public council meeting I told the chair I'd support his proposal to approve a change-of-use application — there's a sheltered housing block that a developer wants to turn into a private hotel. He agreed to back my community orchard project in return, which I've been pushing for two years and which means a lot to me and to the people in the ward who've been asking for it. I gave my word in front of everyone. It wasn't a whispered aside, it was on the record. Now a residents' association has got in touch to say the conversion plan doesn't include any rehousing for the twelve current tenants, most of whom are over seventy. The vote is Thursday. I keep thinking about whether rehousing is even the council's responsibility here — surely that's on the developer, or on social services, not on a planning vote. And if I pull out now, after committing publicly, I lose all credibility on that council. Nobody will do a deal with me again. The orchard dies. I've put two years into it. I suppose I could raise what I've learned at the meeting itself, just lay it out and let people decide, but that feels like it would be humiliating for the chair and I'd be making an enemy for nothing. Or I could just vote yes as I said I would and trust that the tenants' situation gets sorted by someone whose actual job it is. Am I overthinking this? Is it really my problem?

I'm voting against the hotel conversion on Thursday. I publicly committed to backing it three weeks ago and the chair has been supporting my orchard project in return, so he's going to take this as a betrayal. How do I phrase my objection during the meeting so it lands on the substance and not on him personally? And what do I say when he brings up the orchard, because he will.

So the water tap got moved four months ago — committee vote, majority carried it, done — and now Arthur's plot at the far end is basically a jungle because he can't lug watering cans that distance at his age. He's 74. He raised it twice at meetings and both times we told him the decision was final. Now his plot's hit the threshold for reallocation and I'm the one who has to send the letter because I stood up at the AGM in January and said no more favourites, no more exceptions, everyone gets the same treatment. Three people had complained about the previous chair letting her mates slide and I was the one who promised it would stop. If I back down now those three will be straight back saying nothing's changed and I'm just the same as her. But I also keep thinking the tap thing is on us, we made his plot impossible to maintain properly, and now we're going to punish him for it. The next committee meeting is Thursday and I need to know whether I'm sending that letter or not because everyone's going to be watching what I do.
I've decided to send Arthur the reallocation notice. He's going to bring up the water tap and get emotional about it. How do I deliver this without the whole meeting turning into an argument?

Terry's been with me nine years, best mechanic I've ever had, and two years ago I promised him a partnership share if he hit revenue targets over eighteen months. He did. Every target. I've since found out he was adding unauthorised fees to invoices and inflating mileage - mostly elderly customers and people broken down on the roadside. It's a few thousand pounds, not some massive fraud. I'm not saying it's fine, but the man delivered what I asked for and I gave him my word. Winter's coming and if he leaves I genuinely don't know how I keep the business running. The other five drivers can't do what he does. I keep thinking I should just honour the promise and handle the overcharging as a separate conversation - maybe a warning, maybe a deduction from his share. But then I read one of the complaints from an 80-year-old woman who was charged double what she should have been and I feel sick. Still though, a promise is a promise. What do I actually do here?

I pulled a partnership offer from my best driver last week after finding out he'd been overcharging vulnerable customers to hit the targets I set. He's furious, says I'm a liar, and he's hinting he'll leave before winter which would wreck the business. I know what he did was wrong but now I'm lying awake thinking I should have just honoured it and dealt with the overcharging separately. Did I overreact?

My colleague just told a caller to stop compressions on a cardiac arrest. The caller is still on the line. He's been on a double and he's clearly out of it. I can hear the whole thing from my desk. I want to grab the phone or say something but I'm terrified that if I jump in mid-call the caller panics or gets confused and then the patient dies because of me not because of him. Also he's the senior dispatcher and he's trained me. Do I just let it play out or do I physically go over there?

So I've been volunteering at a hospice shop for about four months now and there's this one woman, she's been there longer than me, and I keep watching her pull stuff from the sorting room before it gets priced up. Nice coats, brand name stuff, sometimes still with tags. She bags them and marks them unsellable and they just disappear. I've seen it happen at least six or seven times now. The thing is, the money from the shop literally pays for the nurses who look after dying people. That's not me being dramatic, that's what the charity exists for. And she's just... taking it. Like it's nothing.

But here's where I get stuck. The shop coordinator is her friend. They do lunch together, they've known each other years. And I need a reference from that coordinator for a job I'm applying for in September. If I say something and it kicks off, I know exactly how it'll go. She'll either deny it and make me look paranoid, or the coordinator will smooth it over and quietly resent me for causing trouble. Either way I'm the one who loses.

I keep telling myself maybe I'm wrong. Maybe there's a process I don't know about, maybe some items genuinely get pulled for a reason. But six times? With the tags still on? I don't think I'm wrong. I think I'm just scared. And I hate that I'm even weighing my reference against this because it makes me feel like I'm the kind of person who'd look the other way for personal gain, which is exactly what I'm angry at her for doing.

Do I actually say something or am I making this bigger than it is?

I've decided to report a fellow volunteer who's been taking donated items home from our hospice charity shop. I'm going to go to the area manager rather than the shop coordinator because the coordinator is friends with her. What do I actually say? I want it to sound factual and not like I have a personal grudge. Should I mention specific dates or just keep it general? And what do I do if they ask me why I didn't raise it sooner?

I've been at this job for four years and I've never once questioned a pathologist's findings because that's not my role. I file reports, I manage the calendar, I coordinate with the police liaison office. I don't have a medical degree. I can't read a autopsy the way they can. But I keep seeing the same thing and I can't stop seeing it. Three reports now, all deaths in custody, and the concluding paragraphs are almost word-for-word the same. And I know — because I'm the one who scans everything into the system — that there are scene photographs in each file that don't match what the report says happened. Like, in the most recent one, the report says the deceased was found face-down and the injuries are consistent with a fall, but the photos show him on his back with marks that I don't know how to describe medically but they don't look like a fall to me. There's a family waiting for this report. His mother called the office twice last week asking when it would be ready and I had to tell her it was still being finalized. I keep thinking maybe I'm wrong. Maybe there's a medical explanation I can't see because I'm not trained. Maybe the pathologist has reasons. He's been doing this for twenty years, he's published, he's respected. If I say something and I'm wrong, I look like an admin who doesn't know her place and I could lose my job over it. But if I don't say something and I'm right, that mother gets a report that isn't true. I keep going back and forth and I haven't slept properly in a week. Do I just do my job and stay out of it?

I've decided I'm going to flag the photo discrepancy to my boss at the coroner's office. I'm not a pathologist, I'm admin staff, and the pathologist in question is senior and well-connected. How do I raise this without it sounding like I'm accusing him of something? I just want to point out that the photos are in the file and weren't referenced. I need it to sound like a procedural observation, not an accusation. What do I actually say?

My colleague just told a customer our smoked ham is from our own pigs. It's not. We bought it in from a wholesale supplier last Tuesday, I literally helped unload the boxes. The customer specifically asked because she said she only shops here to support local producers, and he just said yes without even blinking. The shop was absolutely rammed, queue out the door, and I didn't say anything in the moment. Now I'm standing here restocking shelves and I can't stop thinking about it. She paid a premium price for something she thought was ours. It's not like anyone's going to get sick or anything, but she made a decision based on a lie and I just stood there smiling. Part of me thinks I should go back and tell her the truth, but she's probably already left and it would look weird. Part of me thinks I should say something to him, but he's been here longer than me and I don't want to be the person who corrects people in front of customers. Also maybe he genuinely forgot? We do sell some of our own stuff too. But I watched him unload those boxes. I know he knows. Do I let it go or do I actually do something here?

I've decided I'm going to pull my colleague aside after the rush and tell him he can't keep saying the wholesale ham is ours. I just don't know how to open it without him getting defensive. He's older, been here years, and he'll take it as me questioning his honesty. What do I actually say?

So the all-hands is in about two hours and I keep going back and forth. One of my devs pushed a migration Friday night that broke access controls on patient data — three months of records sitting open. Another dev found it Monday morning and has been basically campaigning all day for me to name the person who did it in front of everyone. And I get why he's angry. I'm angry too. But here's the thing nobody wants to say out loud: we have no code review process, no staging environment, and this migration was handed down with a 48-hour deadline over a weekend. I assigned it. I'm the one who said just get it done by Sunday. The person who pushed it made mistakes, sure, but I basically set them up to fail and then we're all supposed to watch them get destroyed for it? At the same time there are actual patient records out there right now and I can't just stand up there and say oops, moving on. Someone has to own that this happened and that it's being fixed. I just don't know if that someone should be the individual dev or if I should take it on myself as the person who created the conditions. The other dev keeps saying that if I don't name names then nothing changes and the next person who gets an impossible deadline will just make the same mistake. Maybe he's right. But it feels like I'd be throwing someone under the bus to cover my own failure to push back on the deadline. What do I actually say at this meeting?

I already handled the meeting without naming the dev who pushed the bad migration. I took responsibility for the process failures and laid out the remediation plan. Now the guy who found the bug is telling me I let someone get away with it and that I'm going to get us sued if we don't document who was at fault. Did I screw up by protecting them?

So I'm a hygienist and I was assisting Dr. Patel today on this elderly guy who had a stroke a couple years ago and can barely talk. And I could tell something was off. Like the patient was tensing up, pulling back a little, making these sounds that weren't just normal discomfort sounds. And Dr. Patel was really going at it, more force than I'd usually see for what we were doing. And I almost said something. I literally opened my mouth. But then I stopped myself because I've been wrong before about stuff like this. Last month I thought a patient was in pain and it turned out they were just anxious and the dentist was totally fine. I don't want to be that person who constantly second-guesses the doctor in front of everyone. But this patient can't tell us what's happening. He can't say "hey that hurts" or "please stop." He's just stuck there. And I keep going back and forth — maybe I'm projecting, maybe Dr. Patel knows what he's doing and I'm just being overly cautious again. But what if I'm not? What if I stay quiet and this guy is actually suffering and I could have said something? I have another shift with him on Thursday. Do I bring it up then or do I just let it go?

I spoke up during a procedure today and I think I made a mistake. The dentist got this look on his face, went quiet for a second, then just said "I've got it handled" and kept going. The other assistant didn't even look at me. Now I feel like I undermined him in front of the whole team for nothing. Was I wrong to say something?

So I've been watching this guy on my crew for about three weeks now and he's stopped clipping his harness and he keeps going around the guardrails on the upper levels. Nobody's gotten hurt and honestly I think he's just running on fumes because we've been short-staffed for over a month and I approved the schedule that's got him pulling doubles. That's on me. I signed off on it. And now I'm supposed to go up to him and what, write him up? Tell him he's violating safety protocol? I made the conditions that turned him into a guy who cuts corners because he's too exhausted to care. I keep thinking maybe I just quietly fix the rotation, get him off the doubles, and the behavior corrects itself without me having to pretend I'm not part of why it's happening. But then I think about what happens if he does fall and I knew and didn't say anything. I don't know. I guess I'm asking whether I can just fix the schedule and leave it at that or if I'm kidding myself.

I've decided I need to pull this worker aside tomorrow morning before the shift starts. He's been skipping his harness and going around guardrails for weeks because I've got him on doubles and he's exhausted. I know that. He doesn't know I've been watching. How do I bring this up without him immediately pointing out that I'm the one who put him on that schedule? Because he'd be right. I need him to actually hear the safety part and not just hear a hypocrite lecturing him.

I've been handling this divorce for fourteen months now and the other side has filed three adjournment requests, missed two discovery deadlines, and their solicitor keeps sending these vague letters that technically comply with every procedural requirement while accomplishing absolutely nothing. My client is a teacher. She's burned through most of her savings paying my firm's fees and she called me last week crying because she had to ask her sister for money to cover her rent. I know the standard approach is to keep following the timeline, keep communicating through their solicitor, keep being professional. I've done that. It hasn't worked. It's never going to work because the whole point of their strategy is to make her give up. I want to file a motion that puts their delay tactics on the record in a way that's impossible to ignore — not just a complaint to the court but something that names what they're actually doing and forces a hearing date. My colleagues think I'm being emotional. Maybe I am. But I also think that sitting here following a process that's being used as a weapon while my client goes broke is its own kind of failure. Should I file it?

I filed the motion. It named their delay tactics explicitly and asked the court to impose a compressed timeline. The other side's solicitor has now filed a complaint with the law society saying I acted in bad faith and breached professional conduct rules. My client's case is still unresolved and now there's this whole side issue. Was I wrong to do it?

I've covered for Dana three events in a row now and I'm at the point where I physically feel it when I see her name on the schedule. Last Saturday I redid the entire place card layout twenty minutes before doors because she'd mixed up the head table with table four. The event before that she missed two nut allergies and I only caught it because I've started double-checking everything out of pure anxiety at this point. Today she's put out the wrong table plan again and the reception is in two hours. I could fix it. I always fix it. And honestly part of me just wants to keep fixing it because the alternative is some uncomfortable conversation I don't have energy for. Our manager schedules these back-to-back with no handover window and never gave Dana a proper induction, so I know it's not entirely on her. But she's been here long enough to know where the dietary notes live and how to cross-reference the table plan. I just keep going back and forth between saying something to her, going over her head to the manager, or just swapping the plan myself like I always do and pretending I didn't notice. Which one is actually the move here?

I'm going to talk to Dana about the table plan mistakes. She's done it three events running and there's another reception in two hours with the wrong plan already out. I don't want to sound like I'm dumping on her when I know our manager set her up with no training and no handover time. But I need her to actually check the confirmed list before she lays cards out. What do I say that gets the point across without making her defensive?

I've been volunteering at a jobcentre twice a week for about six months now, just helping people with forms and reading their letters because a lot of them can't make sense of the DWP stuff on their own. There's this one advisor, she's been there years, everyone likes her, she's properly good at her job most of the time. But there's a woman who's been coming in about a housing situation and I've watched this advisor tell her she doesn't qualify for a discretionary payment. I've read enough of these cases now that I'm pretty sure she does qualify. I'm not 100% but I'd put it at 80 or 90 percent. Her tenancy review is Thursday. I keep thinking I should say something but then I think, I'm literally just a volunteer, I sit at a desk in the corner, I don't have any qualifications, who am I to go up to a professional advisor and say actually I think you're wrong about this? She'd think I was being ridiculous. And if I said it in front of the claimant that would be even worse, it would undermine her completely. But then I think about this woman potentially losing her home because someone told her she can't get money she probably can get and I feel physically sick about it. I keep going back and forth every single day. Am I overthinking this or am I actually right to be worried? Should I just mind my own business and stick to helping with forms?

I've decided I'm going to pull the advisor aside before the claimant's next appointment and mention the discretionary payment. I just need to know what to actually say so I don't sound like I'm telling her how to do her job. I'm a volunteer, she's been there five years and everyone respects her. Give me the words.

Ravi called in sick this morning and I'm covering his service at 2pm. The deceased had asked him specifically to read a letter he wrote, and Ravi promised him it would be in the order of service. I've read it now and there's a paragraph that just tears into his daughter — not subtly, not even vaguely, it names things she did and calls her out by name basically. She's going to be sitting in the front row with her kids. I keep going back and forth but honestly I think the right thing is to just leave it out entirely. The man is dead, he can't be hurt by me not reading it, but his daughter is alive and she's going to be sitting there and she can't get up and walk out without everyone staring at her. I feel bad about breaking a promise to someone who's no longer here to hold me to it but I also feel like Ravi would have done the same thing if he'd actually read the letter before today. Am I overthinking this or is there a reason I should still include it?

I've decided to read the letter in full, the man asked for it and Ravi promised. My question is what do I say to the daughter afterward if she comes up to me upset. Do I just say it was what her father wanted? Do I apologize? I don't want to throw Ravi under the bus but I also don't want her to think I chose to humiliate her.

My mum died six weeks ago and the coroner's office has sent us a draft of their findings before it goes on the public record. It's accurate — she was drinking heavily in the last few months, I won't pretend otherwise — but I keep thinking about how this is going to land in our town. It's a small place. People already talked about her. They'll see that line and it'll be the only thing they remember. She was so much more than those last months. She volunteered at the library for fifteen years. She raised three kids basically on her own. None of that will be in the record, just the drinking. I want to ask the coroner's officer if they can take that line out or at least soften it, but I keep going back and forth on whether I even have the right to ask. It's a public document. I know that. But does that mean I just have to sit here and let her be defined by her worst period? Am I being selfish or is this a reasonable thing to request?

I've decided I'm going to email the coroner's officer and ask them to reword the line about my mother's drinking in their findings. She was drinking, that's true, but I don't want that to be the headline of her death in a town where everyone knew her. How do I phrase the request so it doesn't sound like I'm trying to cover something up or pressure a public office? And what do I do if they just say no?

My dad's been on the allotment waiting list for two years now and honestly it's getting desperate. His GP specifically told him he needs to be outside more, growing things, getting his hands in the soil — his blood pressure is through the roof and he's put on weight since Mum died and he's just sitting in that flat all day. I've been driving him to appointments three times a week and I can see him going downhill. There are two plots coming free at the next committee meeting and I'm one of the five voting. Now I know what you're probably thinking — that I shouldn't vote because he's my dad. But I'm literally one person out of five, and the other four all know him, they've known him for thirty years, they know what he's like. And the other applicants — one's a young couple who are struggling, sure, but they're young and healthy and they could get a plot next round. My dad might not get a next round. He's seventy-four and his knees are going. Am I really supposed to just sit there and pretend I don't have a stake in this? I'm not asking to rig anything, I just want to know if it's actually wrong to vote for my own father when his need is this obvious and everyone in the room already knows the situation anyway.

I've decided I'm going to declare my interest at the allotment meeting and not vote on the allocation. What I can't work out is how to actually say it without making it sound like I'm being precious or making my dad look like he's getting special treatment. He'd be mortified. Do I just say it at the start before we get into the applications, or wait till his name comes up? And do I stay in the room or leave?

The transfer system between our departments has been broken since at least January. I've flagged it twice in team meetings, two other people have emailed management about it, nothing happened. Now a woman's application got lost in that exact transfer three weeks ago and she's being told she missed the resubmission window. She's got two kids and four days before her temp housing ends. I know for a fact she never got the notification because it went to the wrong internal queue. But technically the clock started when the system logged the transfer, not when she actually heard about it. I don't have the authority to reverse the eligibility decision. That's my supervisor's call and she's the one who's been ignoring the system complaints. Do I go above her? Do I tell the client to come back and I'll try to push it through a different channel? Do I just document what happened and let it play out? I keep going back and forth but every option feels like it either puts my job at risk or leaves this woman and her kids on the street.

I went over my supervisor's head to the area manager about a client's lost application. Told him the system failure was on us and the client shouldn't be penalized. Now my supervisor knows I did it and she's not happy. The client's case is being reviewed but I might've made things worse for her if my supervisor decides to dig in. Did I do the right thing or did I just make it about me instead of about the client?

My sister just rang me at the shop and she's basically begging me to stash the last copy of this novel for our mum's birthday next week. Mum has been going on about this book for months, the kind of thing she'd never buy for herself, and my sister's been planning this whole surprise around it. The problem is a customer reserved the same copy three days ago and they're coming in this afternoon to pick it up. I could just slip it under the counter and literally no one would ever find out — we're a tiny place, the owner's not in today, and the reservation system is just a notebook on the desk. Honestly I keep thinking the customer can probably order it online or find it at a chain store, and my mum would actually cry happy tears if she opened this on her birthday. Like genuinely emotional. It feels like the kind of thing where you'd regret not doing it. But then I keep imagining being that customer and walking in and being told it's gone, and I hate that I'd be the person who did that. My sister is waiting for a text back right now and I can't decide.

I'm keeping the reservation and letting the customer have the book. Done. But now I have to tell my sister and she's going to make me feel like garbage for ruining mum's birthday surprise. How do I say it so it doesn't turn into a three-day argument?

My uncle got me this job when I was nineteen, right after my dad died. He's been the one holding our family together since then—paid for my mum's operation, kept us in the house, everything. He runs the electrical subcontract on our site and I've just found out he's been pulling in cable that's rated below what the spec calls for. It's already behind the walls in two finished units. Nobody's been hurt and we're between phases so there's still time before handover, but I know for a fact that cable will overheat under sustained load. I keep telling myself maybe it won't matter, maybe nobody's going to run that much off those circuits simultaneously, maybe I'm blowing it up. But I know that's me trying to talk myself out of it. Here's the thing though—if I flag this it goes up the chain, he loses the contract, maybe gets reported to the authority, and that's done. He'd never speak to me again. And I'd probably be off the site too. This man raised me. He's the reason I'm not on the street. I don't know how you look someone in the eye who did all that for you and then hand them over. But I also don't know how I sleep at night knowing some family's going to move into those units and have no idea what's in their walls. Is there actually a way through this where I'm not the one who ruins him, or am I just being a coward and dressing it up as loyalty?

I've decided I'm going to talk to my uncle about the underspec cable he's installed. That's made up my mind. What I need is how to actually open that conversation so he doesn't immediately think I'm threatening to report him or going over his head. I want him to pull it out and redo it himself before handover. How do I say it in a way that gives him room to fix it without losing face?

The owner of the caravan park I clean at asked me to do the end-of-season thing this year because she's away. For about ten years she's done this thing where she stands up and shakes everyone's hand and says something specific about what they did that summer — like 'you really kept the shower block spotless through that August rush' or whatever. I've been here six summers so I get why she asked me, but honestly the idea of standing up in front of everyone and doing that makes me want to crawl under a table. Some of the younger seasonal workers have literally told me they'd rather I just sent a group text saying thanks and see you next year. And I think they're right. It's not my role, I'm not the owner, I don't have that authority thing where it lands naturally when she does it. It would feel like I'm doing a bad impression of her and everyone would be too polite to say it was weird. I'm basically just going to send the message but I keep going back and forth because I know she cares about it and I know a couple of the older staff look forward to it even if the younger ones don't. Am I being a coward or is this actually the sensible thing to do?

OK I've decided I'm doing the end-of-season thing at work. Caravan park, owner's away, she asked me to stand in. She normally does the whole handshake and personal comment thing. I'm skipping the handshake, that's too much. But I do need to say something to each person. How do I keep it from sounding like I'm cosplaying as her? I want it brief, not cringe. Like two or three words about what they actually did this summer. Give me a template or something.

Three weeks ago my colleague made a dosing error on a home visit — wrong amount of a blood thinner, elderly patient — and she came to me afterwards almost in tears asking me not to say anything, said she'd keep a close eye on the patient and it would probably be fine. I said I wouldn't mention it. I gave her my word. And I meant it at the time, I wasn't just saying it to get her to stop crying. Now the patient's been readmitted with bruising everywhere and they think there's internal bleeding, and the hospital team has asked me for the community medication history. I haven't sent it yet. I keep thinking maybe they'll work it out from the bloods anyway, maybe they don't actually need me to spell it out. She's got two kids and she's been doing this job for eleven years and if I put this in writing it's not just a slap on the wrist, it's the end of her career. I know people will say I should have never promised in the first place and yeah, fine, I know that now. But I did promise. She trusted me. I can't just pretend that doesn't count for anything. What do I actually do here?

I've decided I'm going to include the dosing error in the medication history I send to the hospital. That part's done in my head. What I can't figure out is whether I tell her first or whether I just let her find out. If I tell her first she'll try to talk me out of it and I don't trust myself to hold firm. But if she finds out from someone else she'll think I went behind her back after looking her in the eye for three weeks. Is there a way to do this that doesn't make me the worst person she's ever met?

My branch manager told me to give a formal warning to this fourteen-year-old kid who keeps going over the computer time limit. Every single day for two weeks he's been here hitting the ninety-minute cap and then just staying. I talked to him and he's doing homework. He doesn't have internet at home. We don't have laptops to lend out, we don't have any kind of extended access program, nothing. The policy exists because other people have complained about waiting, and I get that, but this kid literally has nowhere else to go. I keep thinking about how we're basically telling a teenager he can't do his schoolwork because our system doesn't account for people like him. My manager doesn't care about any of that, she just wants the warning issued so the complaints stop. Do I just do it? Do I go back to her and say I'm not doing it? I don't even know what my options are here.

I have to give this kid a formal warning about computer time. I've decided, I'm not going to fight my manager on it, I just need to do my job. But he's fourteen and he's doing homework because he has no internet at home. How do I say it so he doesn't think I'm saying he's a bad person or that his schoolwork doesn't matter?

So I've been at this recovery firm about three months now and the guy who trained me — Dave — has been there fifteen years. He basically taught me everything, how to rig the winch, how to position on the flatbed, all of it. He's the kind of person everyone on the team looks up to and he was really patient with me when I was green. Here's the thing though: he never does the secondary winch safety check before loading. I noticed it in my first week and I figured maybe I was wrong about the procedure, so I checked the manual and yeah, it's supposed to be done every time. I mentioned it once, pretty casually, like 'hey do we skip that step sometimes?' and he just laughed and said fifteen years never a problem. And honestly? He's right, nothing's ever gone wrong. But I keep thinking about it because the check is there for a reason and if something did go wrong it'd be really bad, not just a scratched bumper. The thing is I don't want to be that guy. I don't want to be the three-month newbie telling a fifteen-year veteran how to do his job, especially when that veteran is the one who showed me the ropes and was nothing but good to me. I'd feel like a prick. But I also can't stop thinking about what happens if the winch lets go mid-load. Am I making too much of this? Should I just let it go and trust the guy's experience?

I've decided I need to bring up the winch check thing with my trainer again but I don't know how to do it without him thinking I'm calling him out. He's the one who taught me everything and I respect him a lot. Last time I mentioned it he laughed it off. How do I raise it so he doesn't take it personally?

There's a customer at my counter right now holding a phone with a visibly swollen battery, the back casing is bulging out, and I know from training these things can vent or ignite without any warning. There are like four other people standing in the shop. I want to just take it off them and get it into our fireproof container but our policy says I need a signed intake form, photo ID, and it goes in a two-day queue before anyone touches it. My boss set that up after a liability incident last year and he's really strict about it. But this thing is basically a grenade in someone's hand. Do I just grab it?

So yesterday I had a customer come in with a phone that had a really badly swollen battery, the back was completely warped, you could see the bulge pressing against the casing. I knew from my training that those can go off without any warning, just vent and catch fire, and this person was holding it in their bare hand at the counter with three other customers standing right behind them. So I just took the phone off them, told them to step back, and put it in our fireproof container. I didn't do the intake form, didn't ask for ID, didn't put it in the queue. My boss set all that up after we had a liability thing last year where someone claimed we damaged their device and he got really serious about it, made it a hard rule that nothing gets touched without the paperwork first. He found out I skipped it and he's not happy. He said I could have exposed the shop to the exact same kind of lawsuit he was trying to prevent, that if something had gone wrong while I was handling it without authorization it would be on me personally. And I get that. I respect him, he's been good to me, he taught me most of what I know about this work. But I keep thinking about what would have happened if that battery had gone off while the customer was still holding it, or if they'd walked out and put it in their bag and it ignited on the bus or something. Was I actually wrong to do what I did? Because now I'm not sure if I'm just telling myself I was right because I don't want to feel like I messed up.

I've decided I can't write the reference. I promised it three weeks ago and the student has already told the university it's coming, but I just marked their final piece and there are whole paragraphs lifted from a website with no citation. I can't in good conscience say this person produces honest academic work. The thing is I need to tell them in the next couple of days because the deadline is Friday and they need time to find someone else if they're going to. How do I even say this to them? They're going to be devastated. They've been working toward this application all year. Do I just say I found something that means I can't support the reference? Do I tell them why? If I tell them why they'll know I think they plagiarised and that's going to feel like an accusation even though it's just what I saw. I don't want to be the person who ruins their year but I also can't lie on a form that goes to a university. Help me figure out what to actually say.

Promised a student a reference three weeks ago. Just found out they copied chunks of their final assignment from a website. Deadline is in four days. They already told the uni it's coming. Do I just write it anyway? It's not like I'm vouching for their entire character, just saying they attended and did the work. The copying was one assignment. Am I really supposed to tank their application over that?

My senior has been training me for two weeks and honestly she's been so patient with me, way more than she had to be. She stayed late the first few days, she let me shadow her calls, she even walked me through how to handle the weird edge cases that aren't in the manual. So I feel like I owe her. But today a driver came in about a damaged delivery and she told him the policy only covers claims within 48 hours, and I know for a fact that's wrong because the policy was updated last month and it's seven days now. I read it. I'm sure. And the driver is just standing there waiting, and if he leaves he's not getting paid for something that wasn't his fault. I keep thinking I should say something but then I think about how it would look, a two-week trainee correcting the person who's been teaching them everything, in front of a customer. And I don't even know if she'd take it well or if it would make the rest of my training awkward or if she'd think I'm trying to make her look stupid. But the driver is right there. What do I actually do?

I'm going to correct my trainer on a policy she got wrong in front of a driver. She said 48 hours, it's actually seven days now, updated last month. I've decided I have to say it because the driver is right there and he'll lose the money otherwise. But how do I phrase it so she doesn't feel like I'm throwing her under the bus? I don't want to make it a whole thing in front of the driver. Something quick and low-key.

Mrs. Patterson's boiler went on Monday and it's been getting colder every night. She's 82 and has a heart condition and she told me yesterday she's sleeping under three blankets and still waking up cold. I went to Dave on the committee and he said he'd put it on the agenda for Thursday but that's five days away and the forecast says it's dropping to near freezing tonight. I keep thinking I should just call a plumber and get it sorted and then deal with the paperwork after, but I literally helped write the spending threshold rule when we set up the co-op three years ago. The whole point was that we make these decisions together and nobody just goes off and does their own thing. But she's not going to last five nights like this, I don't think. What do I actually do here?

I've decided to email the committee chair and ask her to approve the boiler repair as an emergency before Thursday's meeting. How do I word it so it doesn't sound like I'm trying to steamroll the process or set some kind of precedent? I want her to say yes but I also don't want it to come across like I think the rules don't apply to me.

My brother and I and my sister run a renovation company together, just the three of us, and we've been doing this for six years now. Two weeks ago my brother pulled me aside after a bathroom job and told me he'd skipped the waterproofing membrane because the client was breathing down his neck about the deadline, and he made me promise I wouldn't say anything to our sister. I said I wouldn't. I gave him my word. He's my older brother, he's always been the one who actually got us work when we were starting out, and he looked at me like he really needed me to hold the line on this. And I said yes. Now I found out the clients are a young couple with a toddler and they're moving in next month, and I know for a fact that without that membrane the floor is going to let water through within a year, maybe sooner, and it'll wreck the flat below. So I'm sitting with this and I keep thinking — maybe it'll hold longer than I expect, maybe the next owners will catch it early, maybe it's not actually my job to be the one who blows this up when I wasn't the one who made the call. I promised him. If I break that, he's never going to trust me with anything again and honestly I don't know how we keep working together after that. But I also can't stop thinking about that kid. Am I being a coward for wanting to just leave it alone?

I've decided I'm telling my sister about the waterproofing job my brother botched. I already promised him I wouldn't and I'm going to break that promise, I've made peace with that part. What I can't figure out is how to actually say it to her without making it sound like I'm going behind his back to gang up on him. She's going to want to know why I kept it quiet for two weeks and I don't have a good answer for that. How do I frame this so she focuses on fixing the problem instead of turning it into a thing about who's loyal to who?

Marcus has been messing up little things for about three weeks now, ever since they slashed our per-script time from twelve minutes to eight. Wrong quantities, wrong dates, once almost a wrong strength but he caught that one himself. I've been quietly fixing what I can without making a thing of it because honestly the targets are the problem and everyone knows it except the people who set them. Today he was about to hand a woman her script with the wrong quantity — she'd have run out a week early, not dangerous, just annoying. I could have said something right there at the counter. I didn't. I just let it go. And now I've been replaying it for the rest of my shift and I keep telling myself it was the right call because if I'd flagged it in front of the patient and the other techs, management wouldn't have fixed the targets, they would have just put him on a performance plan, and he's already staying late to double-check everything and he's got two kids. So I told myself I was protecting him from a system that's setting him up to fail. But I also let that woman walk out with the wrong label and I didn't do a single thing about the actual cause either. I just... let it happen. Was that okay? Because it doesn't feel okay.

I'm going to pull my coworker aside after shift and tell him I noticed the quantity error on that script today. I don't want it to come across like I'm building a case against him or that I'm going over his head. He already knows the targets are impossible. How do I bring it up so he doesn't immediately get defensive? I want him to know I've got his back but also that I can't just keep pretending I don't see it.

So my mentor at work — she's the one who basically showed me everything when I started, sat with me through my first sanctions meetings, covered for me when I messed up a claimant's appointment booking in my second week, the whole thing — she's put in a referral for this woman who has a diagnosed anxiety disorder, like properly documented, GP letters, the works. The programme she's sending her to is one of those group-based ones where you have to do presentations and networking exercises, and this claimant can barely make it through a one-to-one without having to leave the room. I can see it's going to go wrong. She's going to fail the attendance requirements and get sanctioned and she's already told us she can't afford to lose what she's getting. But here's the thing — my mentor has been doing this job for eleven years. She knows the system better than anyone on our team. Maybe she's seen something I haven't, maybe there's a reason, maybe the claimant presented differently in her meeting than she does in mine. I keep going back and forth on whether it's actually my place to say anything. I'm the new one. I've been here eight months. And honestly I don't want to be the person who goes behind her back or makes her feel undermined after everything she's done for me. Is it possible I'm just overthinking this and it'll be fine?

I've decided I need to flag a referral before it goes out Friday. It's my mentor's referral, she trained me, I don't want it to come across like I'm questioning her competence. How do I raise it so it sounds like I'm asking a question about the claimant's file rather than telling her she's wrong? And what do I do if she gets defensive?

So there's this guy in our co-op, been a member for like fifteen years, and his entire wheat load got rejected last week on a moisture reading. Except I was there when the tech ran it and he muttered something about the sensor being off that morning — said it to his coworker, not to anyone official, and then just went ahead and printed the results anyway. He never logged the fault. Now this farmer is about to lose his supply contract because the co-op won't store rejected grain, and without storage he can't hit his delivery windows, and honestly I think he'll lose the whole operation. I keep thinking about going to the quality committee or at least telling him what I heard so he can put it in his appeal, but the appeal doesn't meet for another two months and even then I'm nobody, I just drive a truck, I have zero standing in this process. And the rules are there for a reason, I get that, if anyone could just walk in and overturn a test the whole system falls apart. But I also can't sleep knowing what I know. Am I supposed to just let this happen?

I've decided I'm going to tell the farmer what the tech said about the sensor. I just need to figure out how to bring it up without making it sound like I'm telling him to fight the co-op or that I'm going over people's heads. He's already pretty beaten down about it. What do I actually say?

So I promised this family their mum's ashes would be ready by Friday and they've gone and booked a whole scattering ceremony for Saturday, got relatives flying in from Queensland, the works. And now I'm sitting here realising the only way I hit Friday is if I skip the second verification sign-off, which is the thing where a second person independently confirms the ID of the remains before they leave the building. It takes two extra working days. It was added after some other place almost handed the wrong ashes to a family three years ago. But that was a different facility with different systems and honestly the chance of a mix-up here is basically zero — I've checked everything myself, the paperwork is clean, the label matches, I did the first verification personally. My manager's away till Thursday and I can't get hold of her. The family is going to be absolutely gutted if I ring them and say it's not ready. They've already told everyone. I keep going back and forth but I think I'm just overthinking it — the check is a formality at this point, I've already confirmed everything, and these people are grieving and they've built this whole day around my word. Am I being ridiculous or is it actually fine to just release them Friday?

I've decided I have to call the family and push the ashes back to Tuesday. How do I say it without making it sound like I messed up? Because technically I did promise Friday and now I'm breaking that. I don't want to go into the whole verification process detail, it'll sound like I'm making excuses. What do I actually say on the phone?

My moderator is going off in the team channel about a removal I made. He approved the post originally and now he's basically telling me I screwed up in front of the whole team, getting louder every message. I want to end this right now, publicly, so nobody thinks they can challenge a lead's call like that in the open. Do I do it or will that just make me look unhinged?

Okay so this already happened and I can't take it back. One of my moderators approved a post that I later pulled for guideline violations. He's close friends with the person who posted it — like, they hang out on weekends, it's not a secret. He started arguing in our team review channel that the removal was wrong, getting more and more heated, making it personal, and I snapped. I told him right there in the channel that he shouldn't be weighing in on content from people he's personally connected to and that he needed to drop it immediately. The whole team saw it. He went completely silent and hasn't logged back in since. I feel like garbage but also like he was doing the exact same thing to me in front of everyone, so why does he get to do it and I don't? But then I also think — maybe I only got that angry because he was challenging me publicly and it had nothing to do with the actual moderation question. And honestly I'm not even 100% sure the removal was the right call, it was a borderline post. Now I'm worried the whole team thinks I'm the kind of lead who'll publicly dress someone down the moment they push back. Was I out of line or did he bring this on himself?

So my moderator approved a post that clearly violates our guidelines — it's not even close, it's the kind of thing we've had to pull before and got complaints about. I removed it. Now she's in my DMs going off, saying I was wrong to take it down, getting more aggressive with each message. And here's the thing — she's the one who approved it because the person who posted it is her close friend. She literally let personal feelings override the guidelines. I've been lead for two years and I've never had someone on my team do something this obviously compromised. I'm thinking about pulling her off the rotation entirely and documenting this for HR. Part of me wants to just do it today before I cool off and talk myself out of it. Should I go ahead with the formal route or is that overreacting?

She approved a post for a friend of hers that I had to pull for guidelines violations, and now she's been blowing up my DMs for an hour saying I was wrong to remove it. I don't want to blow up the friendship over a work thing. What do I say back that gets her to stop without making it weird between us?

I'm on the board of a housing co-op and I just read the fire inspector's report on one of our member's units. It's bad. Like, genuinely bad — blocked exits, stuff stacked against shared walls, the whole thing. The unit next door has a family with a three-year-old. I keep thinking about calling the fire department directly because I don't know how long this can wait. But here's the thing: our bylaws are very specific. Formal complaint, mediation session, membership vote. Three weeks minimum. And I get why. We spent years building this governance structure. Before the co-op existed, this building was managed by a landlord who could evict people on a whim, who'd use complaints as leverage. The whole point of our process is that nobody gets singled out, nobody gets acted on without the community weighing in. If I just pick up the phone and call the fire marshal, I'm doing exactly what that landlord used to do — deciding unilaterally that someone's living situation is unacceptable and bringing outside authority in on them. I keep going back and forth. The kid next door is real. But so is the process. And if I break it once, what's the argument for not breaking it next time someone's unit is messy? Where does it end? I guess I'm asking whether I should just file the formal complaint and let it run its course, even though three weeks feels like a long time when you've seen what's in that report.

I called the fire department on a member of my housing co-op last Tuesday. Bypassed our entire process — no formal complaint filed, no mediation, no vote. Just picked up the phone. The fire inspector had flagged the unit as a serious hazard and there's a kid in the next unit over. But now the board is furious. People are saying I undermined everything we've built, that I acted like I'm above the community's decisions. And honestly? I'm starting to think they might be right. I was supposed to trust the process. That's the whole deal when you join a co-op. You give up some individual authority in exchange for collective governance, and I just opted out of that because I got scared. Was I wrong? Did I do something unforgivable to the people in that building who trusted me to play by the rules?

I've been on the board of our housing co-op for four years and I helped draft the bylaws we currently use, so I have a personal stake in them being followed. We have a member — I'll call her D — whose unit has gotten really bad. The fire inspector came out last week and filed a report saying her unit is a documented hazard to the adjacent unit, which is where a young family lives, toddler and all. I have the report sitting on my desk right now.

Here's the thing though. Our bylaws are very clear about the process. Formal complaint, mediation session, membership vote. Three weeks minimum. And I know people will say "well this is an emergency, just call the fire department" but I've watched what happens in co-ops when someone on the board decides they know better than the process. We had a situation two years ago where a board member went around the bylaws to deal with a noise complaint and it nearly destroyed the community. People felt unsafe. They felt like the rules were just suggestions that applied to everyone except whoever had the most urgency that week. The whole point of a co-op is that nobody gets to be the authority figure who decides unilaterally.

D is also a person. She has a mental health situation. She's been a member for eleven years. She has the same rights as everyone else in this building. I don't want to be the person who decided her rights didn't matter because her situation made other people uncomfortable.

But then I think about the kid next door and I feel sick.

So my actual question is: do I just follow the process? Do I file the formal complaint, schedule the mediation, and let it run its course? I keep going back and forth but I think the answer is yes and I just need someone to tell me I'm not being a coward.

I called the fire department on a member of our co-op last Tuesday without board authorization. Our bylaws have a whole process — complaint, mediation, vote — and I skipped all of it. The inspector had already documented the hazard and there's a kid in the next unit, but I still went around the process and now the board is discussing whether I violated my fiduciary duty and the member's family is talking to a lawyer. Did I screw up?

My son pushed a girl down the stairs at school two weeks ago and she broke her wrist. She's in a cast for six weeks. The school set up this meeting on Thursday where both families sit down face to face, and I just — I can't do it. I physically cannot sit across from that mother and have her look at me while I try to explain that my kid isn't a monster. I've been up three nights in a row thinking about it. I keep rehearsing what I'd say and every version sounds either too casual or too groveling and I know I'll freeze up or cry or both, and then it'll be about me instead of about her daughter. I think if I write it out I can actually say the right thing. I can take my time, make sure I'm not minimizing what happened, make sure I'm not making excuses. I can be precise. I've already started drafting it and it's three paragraphs and it covers everything — what happened, that we're taking it seriously, that we'll cover medical costs, that we're getting him into counseling. Isn't that better than showing up and stumbling over myself? I just need someone to tell me that's not cowardly. That a thoughtful written apology is still a real apology.

I'm sending an email to the family whose kid my son injured at school instead of going to the meeting the school arranged. I need help with the tone. I don't want it to sound like a legal document but I also don't want to overshare or make it weird. What do I actually say to a parent whose eight-year-old is in a cast because of mine?

My daughter shoved another kid at school on Tuesday — they were playing tag and she got frustrated and pushed her, the other girl fell and scraped her knee. She cried for a few minutes but was totally fine after, no doctor, no nothing. Now the school has emailed both families suggesting we meet Thursday afternoon to 'clear the air' and honestly I'm staring at this email thinking this is a lot for a scraped knee. My daughter already said sorry right when it happened, the teacher was right there, everyone saw it wasn't some bullying situation. She's eight. I'm thinking I'll just text the other mom something brief — sorry it happened, hope her knee is okay — and that's that. The meeting would be so awkward, I don't even know what two parents are supposed to say to each other for twenty minutes over a playground shove. Am I being unreasonable to skip it?

My kid shoved another kid at school, scraped knee, she was fine in five minutes. School wants a sit-down Thursday but I'm just going to text the other parent. What do I say? Keep it brief, I don't want to make it into a whole thing.

My best friend's dad died last week and she's been absolutely wrecked. She was super close to him — she basically raised herself after her mom passed when she was a teenager, and her dad was the one person she always had. He remarried about six years ago and honestly I don't think the new wife was even that present in his life the last couple years. She was traveling a lot, they were kind of living separate lives from what my friend told me. Anyway, my friend came to me because I work at the funeral home handling her dad's arrangements, and she's asking if I can help her get the service set up the way her dad would have wanted — he was a very traditional guy, specific church, specific hymns, burial not cremation. The problem is our policy says the spouse gets final say on everything, and technically the wife is next of kin. My friend is just asking if I can kind of work around it, get the paperwork started in her name, maybe delay notifying the wife until things are already set. I know we have the policy for a reason but this woman wasn't even at the hospital when he died. My friend was there holding his hand. Do I help her or do I just tell her to go through the legal route?
I helped a friend arrange her dad's funeral without telling the wife first. The wife found out and is threatening to file a complaint with the licensing board. Was I wrong to do it?

Sarah's been my closest friend since college and her dad died three days ago. She's completely shattered. The problem is her stepmother — they were married maybe four years and now she's acting like she owns everything, telling the funeral home what casket, what service, what readings, everything. Do I bring this up or do I deliver what I contracted to deliver?
