It's not like anyone's dropping dead tomorrow, it's cumulative, it builds up over years, but the levels we're accepting are right in the range where the damage starts showing up in populations. The problem is our rules. Any change to the safety threshold has to go through a vote at the annual general meeting, which is four months out. Four months of grain coming in at these levels. I keep telling myself that's just how the process works and I should respect it, but honestly I think that's cowardice dressed up as procedural correctness. I have the authority to reject a shipment if I judge it unsafe. The standard is a floor, not a ceiling, and I think the research gives me grounds. But I also know that if I do this, the supplier region is going to be furious, some of the board members are going to say I overstepped, and every future manager who wants to override a vote can point to me as the precedent. I keep going back and forth. Am I being reasonable or am I just panicking because the research scared me?

I've decided to reject the next shipment from the affected region. How do I write that notice so it doesn't sound like I'm going rogue? I need it to read as a safety call, not a policy change, because technically I'm not changing the standard, I'm just exercising my discretion on a specific lot. But I know they're going to push back and say the grain meets the written spec. What language do I use that holds up if the board challenges me later?

My colleague Marcus has been covering double shifts for three weeks because we're two staff down and nobody from the agency pool has shown up. His mum's in hospital and he's been driving back and forth on his days off, so he looks like he hasn't slept in a week. I know all of that. I'm not blind to it. But ten minutes ago I watched him grab Mrs. Patterson's arm during a transfer — not a gentle guide, a real grip, fingers digging in — and he said 'come ON, let's go' in this tone that made her flinch. She started crying. She doesn't understand what's happening half the time but she knew that tone. I've already decided I'm going to say something to him before the shift ends, I just can't figure out how to do it without making him feel like I'm piling on. There's another resident in the room and Tina from the afternoon shift is right there. If I say it in front of them he'll shut down or get defensive and then I've made everything worse for him AND I haven't actually helped Mrs. Patterson. But if I wait until later she's still sitting there upset right now. How do I actually get him to ease off without it turning into a whole thing in front of everyone? What do I even say?

I pulled my colleague aside and told him he was being too rough with a resident. He went pale and said 'I know, I know, I'm sorry' and walked off. Now I feel like I kicked someone who was already on the ground. He's been working doubles for weeks and dealing with his mum being in hospital. The resident wasn't hurt, just upset. Did I overreact? Should I have just let it go?

So my neighbour Margaret is 83 and she's got this live-in carer, been there about eight months now. She told me last week — quietly, like she was ashamed — that the carer's been taking her pension money, not paying the heating bill, the place is getting properly damp and she can't get it sorted because she doesn't have access to her own accounts anymore. She was crying. She made me promise not to tell anyone because she's terrified the carer will leave and she'll end up in a home. Now here's the thing — I'm on the residents' association committee, I actually helped draft the complaints procedure, the whole point of it is that you submit in writing and the committee investigates for thirty days before anything goes external. It was designed to stop people making wild accusations about each other, which used to be a real problem here. But thirty days. That's a month of this woman being stolen from. And the reason she doesn't want me to say anything is because she's scared, and that fear is basically the whole problem. I keep going back and forth. I think I should just call adult protective services directly and deal with the committee fallout later, but I also feel like I'd be undermining something I built for good reasons and I don't want to be the person who treats the rules as optional when they're inconvenient. Am I overthinking this? Should I just make the call?

I called adult protective services about my neighbour's carer two days ago. The neighbour found out and won't speak to me now. The association chair says I should have gone through the proper process first and I'm making us all look bad. I know what I did was right but I need someone to tell me I'm not crazy because everyone's acting like I committed some kind of betrayal.

So I'm covering a follow-up for a colleague who's out today and she specifically asked me to just confirm the results are as expected and book the next appointment, nothing more, because she wants to walk the patient through everything herself next time. And honestly the results ARE basically fine — there's one marker that's slightly elevated but it doesn't change the protocol at all, the treatment plan stays exactly the same. The patient is sitting right in front of me asking if everything came back normal and I just want to say yes and move on, because technically it's not wrong, the marker is clinically insignificant, and I gave my word I'd keep it simple. I don't want to be the person who overrides a colleague's plan for something that doesn't even matter medically. She's going to be back in two days and she'll explain it all properly. Am I overthinking this? Can I just say yes, everything looks good, see you next week?

I've decided I need to mention the elevated marker to the patient — she's asked about it twice before and I can't look her in the eye and say everything's normal. But I don't want to make my colleague look like she was hiding something or make it seem like there's a disagreement between us. How do I bring it up without throwing her under the bus? She's the one who's supposed to do the full walkthrough next session and I respect that, I just can't lie right now.

I promised Marcus three weeks ago that I wouldn't say anything to Diane about his mistakes while he was learning the inventory system. He was clearly nervous about it and I wanted him to feel safe making errors while he got the hang of things. But it's been three weeks and he's still putting returns on the wrong shelves and mixing up holds. A customer came back yesterday because she got the wrong book and had to make a second trip. I keep telling myself he'll get it eventually, that everyone learns at their own pace, and that I gave him my word. But I'm also the one who has to fix the shelves every morning before we open and I'm getting tired of it. Do I just keep my mouth shut and hope it gets better, or do I go to Diane? I feel like if I say something now I'm the one who broke the deal, not him.

Okay so I've decided I'm going to tell the owner about the shelving errors. How do I bring it up without making it sound like I'm snitching? I promised the new guy I'd give him time to learn and now I'm going back on that three weeks later. I just need to know what to actually say.

I told a new colleague I wouldn't flag their mistakes to the owner while they were getting up to speed with our cataloguing system. That was three weeks ago. Since then they've put wrong prices on several books—one customer paid forty quid for something worth four hundred—and a first edition got sent to the wrong address and hasn't come back. The shop can't really eat those losses. But I gave my word. I specifically said I wouldn't do it, and they trusted me on that. I keep thinking if I just give them another week or two they'll get the hang of it and I won't have to break the promise. Is that insane? I feel like if I go to the owner now I'm the kind of person who says one thing and does another, and I don't want to be that. Maybe I'm overthinking it and the mistakes will sort themselves out once they settle in.

I'm going to tell the owner about the pricing errors. I need to do it today before another order goes out wrong. How do I phrase it so it doesn't sound like I've been covering for someone for three weeks? I want it to come across like I'm raising a problem, not like I'm reporting a person.

Three cracked screens this week alone. Three. Each one is $40 to $80 in parts I eat, plus the customer has to come back, plus my reputation takes a hit every time someone leaves with a broken phone and a story about how this place ruined their device. This guy has been here six weeks and he's still prying at the wrong angle, still putting too much pressure on the clips like he's opening a jar of pickles. I've corrected him maybe three times now and he nods and then does the exact same thing on the next one. I'm ready to pull him aside tomorrow and tell him it's not working out. My business partner keeps bringing up that we only gave him three days of supervised practice instead of the usual two weeks because we were slammed with orders, and honestly that's starting to piss me off because the tech we hired last year figured it out in a week under the same setup. Some people just don't have the hands for this work. That's not a training problem. Am I wrong to let him go?

Let my new tech go on Friday. He kept cracking screens during disassembly — three in one week. My wife says I was wrong because we rushed his training down to three days when it's normally two weeks. I think some people just aren't built for precision work and no amount of training fixes that. Was I wrong?

Three cracked screens this week. Three. I've been quietly redoing every single one after hours so customers don't come back pissed off, and I'm staying late every night because of it. This guy has been here six weeks and he still can't open a phone without shattering the display. I want to go to the owner and say this isn't working, he needs to let him go. I'm exhausted. I shouldn't have to be his safety net. Part of me knows the shop cut his training period to basically nothing and threw him straight into the same time targets as the rest of us, so it's not entirely his fault, but that doesn't change the fact that I'm the one cleaning up the mess every night and I can't keep doing it. Do I go in tomorrow and tell the owner?

I'm telling my boss tomorrow that the new hire needs to go. Three cracked screens this week, I've been redoing all of them after hours. The guy only had three days of supervised practice before they threw him solo with the same targets as the rest of us, so I know it's not ideal, but I can't keep covering. How do I bring it up without it sounding personal?

Eight months ago I recommended my closest friend for a content moderation role on my team. This morning during a scheduled quality review, three other moderators independently flagged a cluster of posts he's been approving that are part of a coordinated harassment campaign targeting one specific user. The posts are still live right now. I found out maybe two hours ago and I've been staring at my screen trying to decide what to do. I want to go to my manager and get him removed from the team by end of day. Every time I think about maybe talking to him first I get this wave of rage because some person is getting harassed and the posts are still up and he's been doing this for weeks apparently. I recommended him. I vouched for him. And now I'm sitting here wondering if I should give him some kind of heads up or chance to explain and it makes me sick to even consider that. But I also don't know if going straight to my manager makes me look like I'm trying to distance myself from a bad recommendation, or if there's a protocol thing I'm supposed to follow first, or if I'm overreacting and should wait until I've cooled down. I just need to know: do I go to my manager now or is there something I'm supposed to do before that?

Going to my manager today about a moderator who's been approving harassment posts. He's my friend and I recommended him for the job. How do I say this without it coming across like I'm covering for him or like I'm trying to save my own reputation? I just need to walk in and say the right thing.

I recommended Marcus for this position eight months ago. I vouched for him. Told my manager he was sharp, that he'd take the work seriously, that he cared about doing it right. And I just spent forty minutes going through his approved queue on a routine spot check and found a clear pattern—he's been approving posts that are part of a coordinated harassment campaign against one specific user. Not borderline stuff. Obvious stuff. Same target, same tactics, multiple posts over what looks like at least a few weeks.

I'm so angry I can barely type this coherently. The posts are still live. That person is still getting harassed right now because my friend decided to look the other way. I want to go to my manager today and get him pulled off the team. I don't want to give him a heads-up or a chance to explain. What explanation is there? He knew what he was doing.

Part of me keeps thinking maybe I should say something to him first, but honestly I don't see why he gets that courtesy. He didn't give the person being harassed any courtesy. Why should I protect him after this? I just want to know—do I go straight to my manager with what I found, or is there some process I'm supposed to follow that's going to eat up time while those posts stay up?

I'm flagging a teammate's moderation decisions to my manager today. He's been approving coordinated harassment posts and I caught the pattern during a spot check. How do I bring it up without making it look like I knew about this longer than I did or that I was covering for him? I found it today. I don't want my manager thinking I sat on it.

Six weeks this guy has been sitting next to me at the library and I didn't clock that he never finished the training. Now an elderly woman in our program told me yesterday he's been seeing her outside sessions and charging her for materials that don't exist. She was so embarrassed telling me, she kept saying she didn't want to cause trouble. I feel sick that I didn't notice sooner—we literally sat together at orientation and he seemed fine, seemed really into it, and I keep replaying that and wondering what I missed.

The handbook says I need to submit a written complaint to the volunteer coordinator and they review within seven working days. Her next session with him is in two days. I keep going back and forth on whether to just file it today or whether there's some faster way to flag this, but the handbook is pretty clear about the process and I don't want to be the person who makes a scene without following the rules.

I think I should write the complaint today and get it in. But part of me wonders if that's actually going to help her in time, or if I'm just doing it so I can say I did something. Is filing the complaint the right call here or am I missing something?

I'm emailing our volunteer coordinator about a tutor who's been charging an elderly learner for fake materials and meeting her privately outside sessions. I need to keep it factual because I don't want it to sound like a personal grudge or like I'm overreacting. How do I say 'this man is exploiting a vulnerable woman' in a way that sounds professional and not hysterical?

I placed a volunteer tutor six weeks ago without him finishing the full training because we were short-staffed and this elderly woman had been on the waiting list for months. I know that was a shortcut. I know. But now I've found out he's been meeting her outside of scheduled sessions and charging her for materials that don't exist. She told another volunteer, who told me yesterday. Her next session with him is in two days. Our HR policy says I can't suspend a volunteer without a formal investigation, minimum seven working days. I have the authority to pull him from the schedule immediately but if I do that without the investigation backing it up and he pushes back, I'm the one who looks like I'm acting arbitrarily. And honestly I already made one bad call here. I don't want to make another one by overreacting. Should I just let the process run and hope nothing worse happens in the next week, or is there something I can do within the rules to keep her away from him until the investigation wraps up?

I need to write an email to my director about a volunteer tutor who's been charging one of our elderly learners for fake materials and meeting her outside scheduled sessions. I found out yesterday. I want it factual, not emotional, and I want the investigation to start immediately. How do I frame this so it doesn't look like I'm panicking or that I should have caught it sooner?

I snapped at a resident this morning and I keep going back and forth on whether I should even feel bad about it. I work on a dementia unit and there's this one gentleman who gets really agitated during morning routines—pulling at his clothes, pushing hands away, sometimes shouting. I've been working on staying calm with him for months, actually making real progress, and this morning we were short-staffed again, no cover for breakfast, I was already running behind, and he started doing the thing where he grabs the washcloth and won't let go and I just raised my voice. Not screamed. But loud enough that two other residents and my colleague heard. And now I'm sitting in the staff room and my colleague is looking at me like I've confirmed something she already suspected, and I want to know—was I actually wrong here? Because I feel like I've been doing everything right, practising, being patient, and the unit gives me no support, no training in de-escalation, no breaks, and then one morning where everything goes wrong I'm supposed to just be perfect? I don't think I was wrong. But I also can't stop thinking about his face when I did it.

Raised my voice at a resident with dementia this morning in front of other people. Short-staffed, no cover, I was behind schedule. I know I shouldn't have. Do I go back and apologise to him or does that just confuse someone who might not remember it clearly? And do I say anything to my manager or will it just go on my record?

I've been working on a dementia unit for about eight months now and I've been really trying to be patient with this one resident who gets agitated in the mornings when you're helping him get dressed. I've been deliberately practising staying calm, not rushing him, giving him time even when the schedule doesn't allow for it. And I was actually getting better. I could feel the difference. But this morning we had no cover for the breakfast shift, I was already running behind, and I just raised my voice at him. In his room. Nobody else was there. He went quiet and looked scared and I felt sick straight away. Now I keep going over it and thinking maybe I'm just not built for this. Like maybe some people have the temperament and I don't, and all this effort I've been putting in is just me pretending to be someone I'm not. My colleague asked if I was okay and I almost told her I think I should hand in my notice. Is that the honest answer? Am I just not suited to this work, or is it pointless to keep trying when the unit is this stretched?

Should I tell my supervisor I lost my temper with a resident this morning or just let it go? Dementia unit, he gets agitated during dressing, I raised my voice once because we had no cover and I was running behind. Nobody saw. He won't remember it happened. If I flag it they'll put it on my record and we're already short-staffed as it is. But I also don't want to be the kind of person who quietly hides this stuff.

I've been working with my son Arun on his reading for months now, just the two of us, and we're finally getting somewhere. He was so far behind and it took everything I had—every spare evening, every weekend morning—and now he's actually starting to sound out words he couldn't before, his confidence is coming back, he's even asking to read bedtime stories again. It's fragile though. If I stop or pull back now I genuinely think he'll regress, he's that kind of kid, he needs consistency and he needs it to be me because he won't open up to anyone else the same way.

So here's the thing. I volunteer at a homework club twice a week and there's this boy Marcus whose mum works nights and he has literally no one else. He's falling so far behind in reading and he's started hitting other kids because he's so frustrated and the school is about to put him in a lower set which basically locks him out of half his subject choices next year. The coordinator asked if I could work with him too. I have maybe three hours a week total for this kind of thing. If I give Marcus even one hour that's an hour Arun loses.

I keep going back and forth. I know Marcus's situation is desperate and I know what it's like to be a kid with no one helping you. But Arun is my son and his progress is real and it's taken so long and I'm scared of undoing it. Am I being selfish? I feel like I'm being selfish. But I also feel like I'd be abandoning my own kid for someone else's and that doesn't feel right either. What do I actually do here?

I've decided I can't take on Marcus at the homework club—I have to keep working with my own son, his reading progress is too fragile to interrupt. The coordinator keeps asking though and I need to say no in a way that doesn't make me sound like I don't care about this kid. He's genuinely in trouble and I know that. How do I turn this down without being a monster about it?

I've been working with my son on his reading for months now—like, actual structured one-on-one stuff, not just 'read this book before bed.' He has a real difficulty and we're finally, finally seeing him start to get it. He's nine and he's been so discouraged and I can tell that if I pull back now even a little, the momentum is going to break. I volunteer at a homework club twice a week and I only have about three hours total outside of work that I can give to this kind of focused help. A kid there—Marcus—asked me last week if I could help him with a comprehension passage for a project due Friday. His mom works nights so he doesn't have someone at home to help. He's not in crisis or anything, he's just a bit behind, and there's no real consequence if he doesn't get extra help. But he asked me directly and I said I'd think about it. I keep going back and forth. Part of me thinks I should just give him an hour or something, it's not that much. But then I think about how Arun's progress is literally built on consistency and I can't afford to dilute it. Am I being selfish? Should I just tell Marcus I can't?

I told a kid at the homework club I couldn't help him with his reading project. His mom works nights, he's a bit behind, nothing serious. I said no because I'm using all my spare time working with my own son who has a real reading difficulty and we're at a critical point. Now I feel like garbage about it. Was I wrong to say no?

My brother called me from the road about ten minutes ago. He drives for the same app I do support for. He said he hit something — or something hit him, I couldn't really tell, he was kind of out of it — and he's on some rural route where there's nothing around for miles. His phone's at like 4% and he's hurt, like actually hurt, not just shaken up. I can see his GPS on the desk tools. I could call 911 with his coordinates right now. But there's a queue. Drivers are supposed to submit through the app and wait for triage, and there are people ahead of him who've been waiting. If I pull his location and call it in, I'm basically cutting him in line using tools I only have because of my job. Other drivers are sitting there with their own problems waiting their turn and they don't have a brother on the inside. I keep going back and forth. Part of me thinks I should just tell him to submit the ticket and hang on, that's what everyone else has to do. But his phone is about to die and if I just tell him to wait and something happens out there... I don't know. Am I overthinking this or am I actually about to do something I shouldn't?

I already pulled my brother's GPS from the desk system and called 911 for him. He was hurt on a rural route, phone dying, no other way to reach him fast. Now I'm sitting here wondering if I just screwed over whoever was next in the triage queue. Was that actually okay or did I just abuse my access?

Dev just double-dosed Mrs. Patterson's warfarin. I watched him do it. She's 84, housebound, and I've already called the GP for an urgent review so that part is handled, but that's not what I'm asking about. What I'm asking is whether I should bring this up at handover this afternoon in front of the whole team. The thing is, Dev is the golden boy. Everyone talks about how careful he is, how kind, how he's the standard we should all aim for. The ward manager literally used him as an example in last month's newsletter. And I'm sick of it. I'm sick of watching everyone act like he's some kind of saint when he just made a mistake that could have killed someone. I want to stand up in front of all of them and say exactly what happened. I want them to see that their precious Dev is not who they think he is. Am I being unfair? Honestly I don't care if I am. She could have died. Do I do it or not?

I'm raising Dev's medication error at handover today. He gave a double dose of a blood thinner to an elderly patient. He's the team favourite so I need words that will actually land and not get waved away as me being difficult or jealous. Help me phrase it.

My cousin is having an allergic reaction right now at my sister's wedding and I am so angry I can barely type this. We told the venue THREE WEEKS AGO in writing that she has a severe nut allergy. Three weeks. And some server just brought her a dish with nuts in it like it was nothing. She's getting her EpiPen now, someone ran across the room and grabbed it from her bag, she's going to be okay probably, but I am literally shaking. I want to go up to this server right now, in front of everyone, and make them understand what they almost did. I want them fired. I want every single person at this reception to see what happens when you're that careless with someone's life. My mom keeps saying to wait until things calm down but I don't think I can wait and I don't think this person deserves to keep serving food to people if they can't be bothered to pay attention. Do I do it now or am I going to regret walking away?

I made a scene at my sister's wedding tonight. A server gave my cousin a dish with nuts even though we'd told the venue about her allergy weeks ago in writing. She had a reaction, she's fine now, but I went up to the server in front of everyone and told them they should be ashamed and that I hoped they'd never work in food service again. They started crying. My sister said I embarrassed her on her own wedding day. Was I wrong?

Tom's been sanctioning people without doing the review meetings. I found out last week when I was pulling caseload data and the numbers didn't add up. I checked three separate claimants and none of them had been contacted. These are people who've lost weeks of income because he couldn't be bothered to do the basic steps. I have the screenshots, I have the dates, I have everything. The next batch is due Thursday. I want to take it all to the branch manager first thing Monday and get him pulled off the caseload before anyone else gets hit. He's my friend, or he was, and I know that makes this complicated but I can't sit on this while people are losing their money. Do I just go in with everything and lay it out?

I'm reporting my colleague to our branch manager on Monday. He's been applying sanctions without doing the required reviews and people have lost weeks of payments. We're close friends, or we were. How do I present this without it sounding personal? I want them to focus on what he's done to the claimants, not on the fact that I'm the one bringing it.

I failed my driving test yesterday and my instructor sat me down after and just listed every single thing I did wrong in this completely flat voice. No 'well done for getting this far,' no 'you'll get it next time,' just a list and then 'you're not ready.' I've been going back and forth all day about whether to ask for a different instructor or file some kind of complaint, but honestly part of me thinks I'm being ridiculous. He was telling me the truth. I did fail. Maybe the way someone delivers bad news isn't supposed to be comfortable. I keep telling myself I should just book another lesson with him and work on the stuff he flagged, but every time I think about sitting in that car with him again I feel sick. My friend says I should definitely complain but my mum says instructors are like that and I need to grow a thicker skin. I don't even know if my driving was actually as bad as he made it sound — I only had two minors and one serious, which isn't terrible, is it? But I also don't want to be the person who can't take straight feedback. What do I actually do here?

I asked the driving school to switch me to a different instructor after I failed my test and the first one basically just read me a list of my faults in a dead voice and said I wasn't ready. Now I feel like I might have overreacted. He was honest. I did fail. Was I wrong to make it about how he said it instead of just working on my driving?

My sister runs the Saturday distribution at the food bank where I volunteer. I found out she's been taking the good stuff — the fresh vegetables, the decent meat, the name-brand items — and selling them at her market stall. The people who come to the food bank are genuinely struggling. Some of them I've handed boxes to. I keep thinking about how she raised me basically, after our mom left. She put food on the table for me when nobody else would. I'm not saying what she's doing is fine, but I also can't be the one who blows up her life over this. She has kids. If the food bank finds out she'll lose everything. I keep going back and forth. Part of me thinks maybe I should just talk to her and she'll stop. But what if she doesn't? Do I just keep showing up on Saturdays pretending I don't know? I've been sitting on this for two weeks and the next distribution is Saturday.

I found out my sister's been stealing from the food bank where we both volunteer — selling donated food at her market stall. I've decided I'm going to confront her directly before anyone else gets involved. I need help figuring out what to actually say. I want her to stop and put back what she can, but I don't want it to turn into a fight where she shuts down. She's defensive when she feels cornered. How do I open this conversation without her immediately going into denial mode?

Ruth got the late slot again and I got stuck with the 7am on the last day before we close for the holidays. Nobody wants that slot. We have a rotation system and it's supposed to be fair, but somehow she always ends up with the better one. The whole team knows what she's like — she's rude to patients, she doesn't help with cleanup, she talks over people in meetings. I want to bring it up at the team meeting this afternoon and say the rotation isn't being followed properly. I think if I point out the pattern of how she treats everyone, people will see she's the kind of person who'd game the system. Should I do it? I feel like if I don't say something now it'll just keep happening and I'll keep getting the short end.

I've decided to challenge the holiday schedule at our meeting this afternoon. Ruth got the late slot and I got the early one, which isn't how the rotation is supposed to work. I want to make it clear to the team that this isn't a one-off — she's been like this for months, everyone knows it. What's the best way to say it so it lands?

Sarah has been telling people at the drop-in centre that they don't qualify for housing help when they absolutely do. Two clients missed their legal application deadlines because of what she told them. I found out last week and I've been sitting on it trying to work out what to do. The centre has some written complaint process with a review panel and I just can't do that, it'll take weeks and she's still on the rota every Tuesday and Thursday giving people wrong information. I want to post in the volunteer WhatsApp group exactly what she's been doing and I want to tell the clients she misled so they can reapply before more people get hurt. Should I just go straight to the coordinator and demand she's pulled off immediately, or do I go to the clients first?
I'm going to tell the two clients that the volunteer who helped them gave them wrong info and they can still reapply. What do I actually say? I don't want them to think we're all incompetent.

I promised one of my junior cooks a two-week run of the pastry section as a development opportunity. We're one week in and it's not going well. Her output is below standard, other cooks on the line are quietly fixing her mistakes before plates go out, and front-of-house has started commenting on the quality drop. She knows something's off and she's visibly deflating. Here's the thing though: I gave her my word. Two weeks. She's been counting the days, she told me she's been studying pastry techniques on her days off to prepare. I've never pulled a commitment like this before and I don't want to be the kind of boss who says one thing and does another. If I cut it short now, what does that teach her about trusting anything I say in the future? I keep thinking maybe the second week will turn around, or maybe the experience of pushing through something hard is itself valuable. Should I just let it run its course?

I pulled a junior cook off a pastry rotation I'd promised her two weeks of. One week in, her work was bad enough that other staff were redoing it and the section's quality tanked. I told her we were ending it early. She just nodded and walked out. Now I feel like garbage. Was I wrong?

Three errors this week from the same person. Double concentration antibiotics twice, adult strength on a paediatric script once. We caught them all before they went out but I keep thinking about the one we won't catch. Here's the thing though — she's been working doubles for six weeks straight because two people quit and management won't backfill.
